speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to move a motion under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the importance of a full and complete briefing for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) concerning the situation at Statistics Canada, particularly since the report in the Gazette this morning goes beyond his statement in the House yesterday, and since it is of the importance of the integrity of Statistics Canada, and to remove the shadow over public servants employed there, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):

Mr. Speaker, the legislation to which the right hon. member is referring is the bill which did not, in fact, get final passage before Congress rose and the session ended. Therefore, this legislation referred to in the article is not law in the United States. The hon. gentleman is quite right. There was considerable concern for obvious reasons about its possible extra-territoriality and when I met with Mr. Kissinger originally in New York at the United Nations, I made clear to him

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF POLICY ON INTERNATIONAL BOYCOTTS
speechtext:
Thank you; Mr. Speaker, the government has clarified its position in relation to international boycotts and has strongly affirmed its opposition to discrimination and boycotts based on race, national or ethnic origin or religion. Accordingly, the government will take measures to deny its support or facilities for various kinds of trade transactions in order to combat any discriminatory effects which such boycotts may have on Canadian firms and individuals. These measures will not, of course, apply to any boycott accepted by Canada but will clearly apply to such discriminatory aspects as there may be to any other international boycott.
The type of transactions against which the government will take action are those which would, in connection with the provisions of any boycott, require a Canadian firm to: engage in discrimination based on the race, national or ethnic origin or religion of any Canadian or other individual; refuse to purchase from or sell to any other Canadian firm; refuse to sell Canadian goods to any country; or refrain from purchases from any country.
While Canada seeks friendly relations with Arab states and with Israel, Canada also reserves the right to respond to commercial policies of other nations according to its own practices and values. Consequently, the Canadian government will deny its support or facilities, including the support of its trade missions abroad, in the case of any transaction involving boycott undertakings of the type described above.
October 21, 1976

Given that in many parts of the world, including the Middle East, denial of Canadian government support for a particular transaction imposes very serious handicaps, such as those relating to contact with foreign officials, market information and Canadian government financing, it is considered that denial of such support will be an effective deterrent to co-operation with discriminatory provisions of an international boycott.
Canadian firms may decide nonetheless to agree to certain boycott clauses and forgo Canadian government support for the projects concerned. All Canadian firms, however, whether they accept boycott clauses or not, will be required to report all instances of their complying with boycott provisions. Information obtained from such reports will be made available to the public.
The government recognizes that Arab countries consider their boycott of Israel to be a legitimate economic weapon in view of the continuing state of war between Arab countries and Israel. Canada, however, seeks to improve its relations and to develop its trade in peaceful goods with all nations. Any discrimination against Canadian firms or individuals is contrary to Canadian concepts of fairness and the government is determined to ensure that any such discriminatory aspects are not in any way supported by government programs.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF POLICY ON INTERNATIONAL BOYCOTTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement by the government with respect to the Arab boycott is overdue. Opposition to any boycott which is pursued on grounds of racism or prejudice should be a principle of foreign policy. It should not be a last minute position drafted in a context of ambivalence. And, ambivalence there is in this statement. The first paragraph of the statement contains the following statement:
These measures will not, of course, apply to any boycott accepted by Canada . . .
I am sure the minister will want to clarify that sentence, by saying if Canada is about to indulge in a boycott against certain nations and, if it is, which nations they are. There is clear ambivalence at the end of the statement, which reads:
... the government is determined to ensure that any such discriminatory aspects are not in any way supported by government programs.
I just wonder whether this does not add a new perception to the programs and activities of CIDA. I am sure the minister will want to clarify this point a little later and explain if CIDA and our trade missions are going to be involved in such a boycott or if this is a veiled threat.
The new Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) should not be held responsible for the procrastination of this government in coming forth with a statement about the Arab boycott. In fact, no other minister has been as open, forthright and co-operative with the opposition. This augurs well for the future. I recognize that and I commend him for his attitude.
However, I say to him through you, Mr. Speaker, foreign policy is more than the drafting of pragmatic statements by
International Boycotts
pragmatic people. It must be the elaboration of principle on behalf of the nation. The people of Canada care more about bread and butter issues, inflation and unemployment, than they do about foreign policy. Nevertheless, foreign policy affects the way in which a nation weighs itself and what a nation stands for.

I understand the necessity for the federal government to protect the commercial interests of Canada and to maintain friendly and business relations with Arab countries now that they are playing a new and decisive role within the world economic community. I do understand also the need for the government to seek information and to evaluate the political and economic consequences of a decision whose importance shall not be minimized. But mercantilism should not be the only rule of a country which is concerned with morality. Now the Arab boycott is one of those cases where Canada cannot but stand firm as far as principles are concerned. It is in the international community's interest that our action discourage measures which might unduly and unjustly affect the interests of Canada, of Israel and of Arab countries themselves.

The statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of May 8, 1975, to the effect that this type of practice is alien to everything the government stands for and, indeed, to what in general Canadian ethics stand for did not prevent, for example, the Canadian Export Development Corporation, a Crown agency, from allegedly conniving in the boycott when being called upon to account for its actions and without being ordered to stop circumventing the government's stated policy.
Instances have been cited where this Crown corporation is alleged to have insured loans to Canadian companies dealing with Arab countries and complying, willingly or not, with the boycott against Israel. I ask the question, and I am sure the minister will answer it later, have those incidents been investigated? In any event, to date no denial has been given.
Unrestrained opposition to an Arab boycott is the only position a government of this country could take. Anything else I consider to be a major sellout in principle and in fact. The people have the right to nothing less. The issue of principle in foreign policy requires commitment, international consistency and skill. As Canada moves closer to membership in the Security Council, the minister and the government must assure themselves that their international consistency, both as a cabinet and within the External Affairs Department, is sufficient to protect principle. The delay that accompanied today's statement must leave many Canadians cause for concern.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF POLICY ON INTERNATIONAL BOYCOTTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF POLICY ON INTERNATIONAL BOYCOTTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with the spokesman for the official opposition in saying to the minister that it is regrettable it has taken so long for the government to make any kind of statement on a very basic principle, the question of boycotting of Canadian companies by Arab countries or any other country on the basis of race,

October 21, 1976
International Boycotts
religion or colour. There is a strong feeling among many people in this country that part of the reason for the delay has been the fact that senior officials in the department are hostile toward the state of Israel. I refer the minister to press reports which have detailed the situation.
The minister said "the government will take measures to deny its support or facilities for various kinds of trade transactions in order to combat any discriminatory effects which such boycotts may have on Canadian firms and individuals." All the minister is saying is that the government will apply to Canadian companies doing business outside Canada what is now the law in Canada. We have federal and provincial fair employment practices legislation which prohibits discrimination against Canadian citizens on the basis of race, colour or religion. The government is now prepared to apply the same principles to Canadian companies doing business outside Canada.
The minister went on to say he would do this by refusing the assistance of the government to companies with regard to "contact with foreign officials, market information and Canadian government financing". He states that "denial of such support will be an effective deterrent to cooperation with discriminatory provisions of an international boycott".
The bulk, if not all the business done by the Canadian corporations with Arab countries is done through multinational corporations whose head offices are in the United States, Great Britain, Holland or South Africa. They do not need Canadian government assistance to make contacts, obtain market information or financing, although on occasion they have added icing to the cake by using Canadian financing. Therefore, we do not believe that this kind of action by the Canadian government will have a serious effect on cutting back, let alone preventing Canadian companies from dealing with Arab countries.
The minister said, in the last paragraph of his statement, that "any discrimination against Canadian firms or individuals is contrary to Canadian concepts of fairness". However, he avoided saying that the Canadian government will take legislative action to prohibit that kind of transaction. There will be no legal sanctions against doing business with Arab countries and Arab governments. As far as we can tell, the corporations will simply ignore the feelings expressed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson).
We do not understand why the government of Canada does not enact legislation similar to that now before the United States Congress, and I believe it would be supported by all opposition parties, prohibiting Canadian companies from doing business which requires a boycott by Canadian companies of countries recognized by the United Nations and Canada or of discrimination against Canadian citizens on the basis of race, colour or religion. I urge the minister to give very favourable consideration to bringing in such legislation.
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF POLICY ON INTERNATIONAL BOYCOTTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I commend the minister for apologizing because his statement was
[Mr. Orlikow.J
late. I would, however, address one critic to him. We hope this will not happen again and that if the minister has some difficulty asserting himself within his department, which I do not believe, he will also try in the future to send us his statements in French. If we are to have bilingualism in Canada, I think we should try at least to begin in the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, what strikes me first is the lead paragraph of that statement which reads as follows:
The government has clarified its position in relation to international boycotts and has strongly confirmed its opposition to discrimination and boycotts based on race, national or ethnic origin or religion.
[ Translation]
Unfortunately I realize that the government has followed inconsistent policies in external affairs. Today it has stated that it is against a boycott of countries on racial grounds, but in various circumstances in the House and through its former Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) at the United Nations, it has supported resolutions for an international boycott on racial issues.
I am referring to South Africa and Rhodesia. Canada has supported the boycott.
Mr. Speaker, the members of the Social Credit Party of Canada do not believe in economic blackmail such as a boycott to which countries can resort one against the other because no country in this world up to now has succeeded in having an efficient boycott. We remember quite well that some countries advocated an economic boycott against Germany, but to no avail. An economic boycott was declared against Cuba but to no avail. The same was once done against South Africa, again to no avail. In Rhodesia, which was supposed to be boycotted by the United States and Canada and where American companies could not do business, I personally saw some heavy equipment worth millions of dollars from well known American agricultural companies which were doing business while the United States were officially boycotting that country.
Mr. Speaker, economic boycott is nothing but a sort of blackmail, and when a country includes this in its foreign policy, we eventually discover that this same country carries out its trading through the back door of its warehouse, through the back door of the country or through another country.
All of this, Mr. Speaker, to say that we fully support the statement the minister made this morning to the effect that Canada will not participate in this type of international economic blackmail and will not support any boycott against Israel or any Arab country. We therefore support this statement and ask the minister to be consistent from now on when he talks about economic boycott on racial matters.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF POLICY ON INTERNATIONAL BOYCOTTS
speechtext:
Before directing my question to the minister, Mr. Speaker, I want to state in all fairness, following the statement made by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau), that we have indeed received the

French text, in excellent French as a matter of fact. We have received this text, I have it before me and it ought to be on the desk of the hon. member for Shefford by now. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF POLICY ON INTERNATIONAL BOYCOTTS
speechtext: Perhaps I can assuage the hon. member's concern by putting that, in a sense, in the past tense. The object of that line was to make it clear that we were not now rejecting the boycott of Rhodesia which was approved by the United Nations and to which Canada subscribed. I suppose there could be similar circumstances in the future-I am not anticipating any at the present time-and this is specifically designed to cover a situation where the United Nations, through the Security Council, did impose a boycott to which the members, including Canada, subscribed. The words to which the hon. member referred are meant to deal expressly with such a situation.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF POLICY ON INTERNATIONAL BOYCOTTS
speechtext: Is it the intention of the government to deprive a country of aid which it has been receiving from CIDA, should that country become part of the boycott?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF POLICY ON INTERNATIONAL BOYCOTTS
speechtext: I cannot conceive of a situation where aid through CIDA would be involved. There might be one where a Canadian company was supplying goods or services in some form or other. subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF POLICY ON INTERNATIONAL BOYCOTTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have two questions for the minister. He has just told us that CIDA is not involved. I do not see, looking at the document, that there is any reference to withdrawing support from countries. It uses the words "any discrimination against firms and individuals". Possibly the hon. member could read that into it but, once again, I say there is no intention and no thought of involving any CIDA operation. The type of program to which

the statement makes reference covers government financing of various kinds which, contrary to the view expressed earlier by one member opposite, form a substantial part of doing business in many areas of the world, including the Middle East. subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF POLICY ON INTERNATIONAL BOYCOTTS
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister whether he would address himself to the underlying reasons which caused the boycott in the first place. I refer to the spread of racism which is severely affecting the United Nations today and which has put the United Nations in crisis. May I ask what the Canadian government is doing, not only by way of imposing a boycott but constructively and positively, to use its good offices to help the United Nations stop the spread of racism which is so seriously impairing international relations?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF POLICY ON INTERNATIONAL BOYCOTTS
speechtext: I can only reply in a general way to that question today, but I would be glad to let the hon. member have specific instances of occasions in which we have spoken out against racism in all its forms. Certainly, at the United Nations this year, if the hon. member would do me the honour of reading my speech, he will see I made some strong comments in that direction. We have participated in a number of discussions in the UN and elsewhere making known our views against racism. We have made our position abundantly clear. We have, of course, simultaneously rejected out of hand any effort to link racism with Zionism.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF POLICY ON INTERNATIONAL BOYCOTTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that once a boycott has been set in place by a group of nations it is not likely that they will withdraw from that position, and that only sufficient warning as to what the position of the Canadian government will be could have any real deterrent effect-and with all courtesy to the minister I doubt that this somewhat milk and water statement by the government today will be a very effective deterrent-I want to ask the minister two questions. I will ask both questions now to save the time of the House.
First, is the government prepared to make it clear to companies operating in Canada and to Canadian companies that, in the event of a boycott, the Canadian government will introduce legislation making it illegal to join in a boycott that is based on race, colour or religion?
Second, is the Canadian government prepared to make it clear to any nation, particularly to the Arab nations at this time, that Canada will not allow this repeated type of international blackmail to go on and will take retaliatory measures, measures that will be fairly draconian? It seems to me that unless the government is prepared to take action along those two lines we are liable to find ourselves in a very unfortunate situation and it will be too late then to issue any warnings. I think the Arab nations ought to know in advance, and that companies in Canada ought to know in advance, that if they

October 21, 1976
International Boycotts
co-operate in such a boycott the government proposes to move and to move very firmly. I would ask those two questions of the minister.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF POLICY ON INTERNATIONAL BOYCOTTS

Mr. Speaker, I think I have no problem replying in the affirmative on the principles about which the hon. member has queried me. I think there is within the statement-I regret that he does not feel it is as strong as he would have liked to see-a clear message which I think will be carried to companies in Canada that we do intend to take the kinds of actions to which the hon. member has referred. In other words, we will act.
On the other issue of retaliation-I believe that was his word-regarding foreign countries, this is a somewhat more complex question. Without going into it in detail, may I say I would assume that our leverage or our capacity to retaliate may vary substantially from one country to another. It also seems to me that there is something in the questions put by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) in particular, and also by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche). For example, on the question of foreign aid, this is presumably one form of retaliation that might be possible. But would it be appropriate to cause the ordinary people in certain countries that are participating in boycotts undue suffering as a result of the action of their government? I am not at all certain that I can be as firm on the second point about our reaction to the actions of foreign governments as I can in terms of Canadian companies.
In the case of Canadian companies, the situation is clear. If a company expects to get any form of assistance from the Canadian government-and I repeat that the record shows that assistance is most valuable and in many cases essential- then they must be prepared to forgo, denounce or not take part in any kind of boycott conditions contained in a contract.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have had cause to address the House as Secretary of State, and I would not like this moment to pass without indicating my great appreciation for the letters of congratulation which I have received from many hon. members. I should like to refer in particular to the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) who in his speech last Wednesday was very generous in his compliments to me and indicated the

range and challenge of the position which I hold, which is indeed a difficult one. I would like to single out, also, the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) for his welcome, and in particular the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) for his generous remarks. I have received a flood of letters of congratulations and best wishes from members from all parts of the House, and I would like to thank them for supporting me in my first few challenging days in office.
Since becoming Secretary of State I have travelled a great deal in Canada and many times I have come across that phrase of frustration, of anger, sometimes of bitterness which I am sure many members who visited their constituencies over the summer encountered. I refer to that terrible phrase, "We don't want you to ram French down our throats". I want to say that as Secretary of State I have no difficulty in associating myself with that sentiment. I have no trouble at all, so long as the people who say that are equally prepared to say " ... and we do not want to ram English down the throats of French-speaking Canadians".
If one can make that kind of leap of the imagination and take oneself out of one's linguistic boots for a moment and put oneself in the place of those Canadians who speak the other official language, and say, "It is not my intention to impose on others limitations and restrictions on the use of their language, as I do not want them placed on me," then I think one can begin to grasp the essential thrust of the official languages policy of this government which has been supported on all sides of this House. The official languages policy does not impose obligations upon citizens; what it does is conserve, protect and guarantee language rights.
The official languages policy takes nothing away from English-speaking citizens and nothing from French-speaking citizens. What it confers upon French-speaking people are the same rights that English-speaking people accept for themselves as naturally as the air they breathe-it ensures the use of French for French speakers. In fact, the Official Languages Act is a bill of language rights, not of imposition; it is something that seeks to guarantee opportunities, not to restrict them.
The official languages policy has three basic principles. The first is that a Canadian citizen should have the right to receive services from the federal government in whichever of the official languages he uses. The act confers that right. The second is, it asserts that whether one is an English-speaking Canadian or a French-speaking Canadian, one should have the opportunity to travel this country from coast to coast and have access to one's own cultural community. That is why the government is establishing French-speaking radio and television stations from one end of the country to the other, and also English-speaking radio and television stations within the French-speaking parts of the country. The third principle is the hope that the provinces will provide opportunities and
October 21, 1976

facilities wherever practicable for education in the minority official language of those citizens who wish it.
Those are the three essential strands of the official languages policy, and not one of them limits any opportunity, ability or capacity presently held by Canadians. What they do is expand opportunities for Canadians to live a full life in whichever of the official languages is theirs. In other words, the official languages policy is about equality. That is a basic drive in our country.
Most people who came to Canada were seeking to escape the closed structures of Europe. They came because of opportunity and because they wanted to live in a society in which there was equality, not a society of rank and privilege. With the official languages policy we are trying to ensure linguistic equality. We are trying to ensure that French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians will have equality of use of language in the civil service, and that whether they be Frenchspeaking or English-speaking, Canadians can look forward to a career in the civil service. We are trying to ensure equality of service to citizens who deal with the civil service and the public bodies of Canada, so that whichever is their official language they will be served effectively and quickly in that language.
We are trying to encourage the provinces to provide equality of opportunity for all groups in the educational system so that no one will be deprived or disadvantaged if they wish to maintain their official language and at the same time advance in the educational system. We are trying to ensure equality of access to cultural expression so that the cultures based on those official languages are generally available. The theme is that of language rights based on equality, not of imposition or control. It is an attempt to ensure that no Canadian, no matter which language he uses, will be forced to learn and use the other official language if he does not wish to do so. This is the principle which underlies the attempts we are making.
It is because I believe so strongly in this principle that I regret the position taken by the former minister of defence, the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson). He contends that the time has not necessarily come when we should consider these principles of linguistic equality as part and parcel of the essential fabric of our country. He is concerned that if these principles in some way become entrenched in the constitution, Canadians may regret it and they may wish to have more flexibility in order to remove, alter or amend them. I would say to him, Mr. Speaker, that the time has not only come to make this commitment, but the time came in the 1960s. Through the will of parliament we made our fundamental commitment to equal language rights at that time.
It is not true, as the hon. member asserts, that the policy of bilingualism has created tensions over language in this country. That is, indeed, the reverse of the facts. The policy of bilingualism has been an attempt to deal with tensions in our society, tensions which have long been within the history of Canada and tensions which, if it had not been for the government's response, I believe would have led to the shattering of our country.

The Address-Mr. Roberts

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
One cannot say to French-speaking Canadians, as the hon. member for Winnipeg South would say, that 370 years after the arrival of the first French-speaking Canadians, that 200 years after the Quebec Act which protected language rights, that 100 years after confederation which protected language rights, and that seven years after the Official Languages Act, which protects language rights, as a society we have not determined whether these principles of language rights are essential to the fabric of our society. We cannot say that these essential principles are still something we may wish to consider or to reject-that they are in doubt. If we let pass the opportunity to assert our fundamental acceptance of these principles, it seems plain to me that our country will not be able to continue.
Think for a moment in terms of basic human rights. I cannot believe that the former minister of defence would say yes, there have been experiments with the principle of free expression, freedom of speech, freedom of association; yes, those things were started hundreds of years ago and they have been confirmed in various acts of parliament; yes, they have been considered important by Canadians for many, many years but, of course, we do not want to have them protected in any special way in our constitution; we do not want to make these the essential fabric of our country, because we may wish to change or amend them; we do not want to lock these principles into our constitution. He would not say that, nor would any member of parliament.
I would say the time has come, Mr. Speaker, to accept language rights in this country and to give them the same status and importance that we give to other fundamental human liberties. To try to put the argument to French-speaking Canadians that we should wait to see if these are principles that we are going to accept reminds me of Shaw's St. Joan: "How long, how long, oh Lord, before thy kingdom is ready to receive its saints?" I would say: "How long, how long, oh Lord, will it take Canadians to accept and protect the language rights of French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians as essential to this country?"
I put it in terms of language rights and linguistic equality; I do not like the word "bilingualism" because I think it is inherently ambiguous. When one talks of a bilingual society, one could mean a society in which some citizens speak one language and some citizens another. One could mean a society in which all citizens are expected to speak both languages. The phrase in itself confuses some people. I think many people feel it means that some Canadians are going to be forced to learn the other language whether they want to or not.
I have been told the story, I hope it is apocryphal that there are farmers in Saskatchewan who sincerely believe that some day the RCMP will knock on their door and say, "Your number has come up in the computer; it is time for you to go and learn French." That is the kind of attitude which the word "bilingualism" might be taken to imply. 1 stress "linguistic equality," and "language rights." We are not trying to impose

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. Roberts
anything on anyone. We are trying to guarantee to those who speak one of the official language their ability to maintain their language, maintain their culture and maintain their life in that language.
I think most members of the House of Commons and most people in Canada accept, fundamentally, the language policy which I have described. That does not mean there are not questions about its implementation; I am sure there are. Indeed I, myself, have questions about the implementation of some of the programs which have been designed to give fulfilment to those principles which I have described. We have tried a variety of approaches, many of them experimental. Some of those experiments have worked more successfully than we expected. Some of our experiments have worked rather badly, or less successfully. But it is true beyond doubt that the number of bilingual positions in the civil service has expanded greatly in the last five years, that our exchange program in many ways has been successful, and that our youth programs-on which I shall touch later in my speech-have been extremely successful.
Members of the House of Commons are certainly aware of the experimental programs undertaken in Ottawa-Carleton. Those programs were so widely accepted that there was considerable opposition to any suggestion of their being withdrawn. But some of our programs have not been as successful as we would have liked them to be. We shall look at those. There are some methods which we can look at again. We can assess their effectiveness and, if they are not effective, either make them more effective or dismantle them.
Many members have spoken to me about such things, for instance as the regulations which apply to labelling. On my trip out west I heard criticisms about labelling. I heard that the sometimes rigid, overzealous application of regulations in relation to labelling has been an outstanding grievance. I said out there, and I repeat it in the House, that I think in this area there are nits we should not pick, that there are changes which could be made and which should be made. I know that my colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott), will be looking at the labelling regulations to see if any improvements can be made, to see if he can ameliorate the application of the rules and ensure that they apply only when they will effect, in substance, improvements and not simply outrage and irritate people.
There is also the question of the designation of bilingual positions in the civil service. My colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), spoke about that in his speech in the House. I might simply repeat two things he said. First, may I repeat what he said as reported at page 159 of Hansard for October 18, 1976:
-I can already assure the House, for example, that language training programs will be improved, that the linguistic requirements of positions will be reidentified, and that language standards will be revised.
It is not effective, in the pursuit of increasing our capacities to use both official languages in the civil service, to create unrealistic objectives. I also wish to draw hon. members' attention to one more paragraph in the speech of the President

of the Treasury Board where he mentions unilingual public servants. We must be sensitive about the problems they face, sympathetic to their needs, their desires, goals and ambitions. The President of the Treasury Board cited his own experience. He said, as reported at page 161 of Hansard:
My personal experience makes me particularly sympathetic to the difficulties faced by unilingual public servants-and I am talking about unilingual public servants of both languages. In undertaking my new responsibilities, I certainly intend to see that these difficulties are very carefully examined and that programs and procedures are reviewed in order to minimize them and, wherever possible, to eliminate them.
I associate myself as strongly as I can with the statement of my colleague. It is important, when we seek to achieve justice for those who are both French-speaking and English-speaking, that is, for those who are bilingual-that we do not do this at the expense of justice and sympathy for those in the civil service who are unilingual.
I think we should again look at and make people more aware of the kinds of appeal provisions which enable the Commissioner of Official Languages to review problems which have arisen in the civil service to do with promotion in relation to bilingual positions. In addition to being willing to look again at the implementation of programs, we are prepared, as a government, to expand efforts on what is commonly called the "youth option". I am not too fond of the word "option" because it implies "either or"-it implies that increasing our emphasis on extending language training to the youth of our society might be a replacement for some of our other programs, the diminution of what we are already doing in other areas. I do not see the programs which we are about to undertake as replacing others.
We have, as a government, already been active in this area. I cited briefly the experience in Ottawa-Carleton with experimental French immersion programs which have been extremely successful. Some people think that is easier to do in the Ottawa area, perhaps, than in other areas of the country. If one goes to Calgary one will find there, as well, experimental immersion programs which have been extraordinarily successful. One finds classes of children in the primary years, happily, easily and cheerfully talking to each other in French as if it were the most natural thing in the world, and benefiting from that experience in the other language. These are experimental programs, but they are certainly not unique. We have embarked upon a variety of programs which are directed basically at younger people. We are trying to make it easier for the next generation to acquire second language skills; easier than it was, perhaps, for many of us.
The bursary and fellowship programs which were established in my department are oversubscribed in every province. There has been a significant increase in the number of elementary school children enrolled in second language instruction across Canada. More and more students are studying French, and for a longer time. The enrolment of children at the elementary level in French second-language programs across Canada has been increased by over 25 per cent during the past five years. The most dramatic increase has taken place in British Columbia, where the enrolment is up almost 200 per
October 21, 1976

cent. In other provinces, between 1970 and 1975 one finds French second-language programs increasing dramatically. For instance, in Newfoundland enrolment increased by 52 per cent; in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, by more than 120 per cent; by almost 25 per cent in Ontario; over 20 per cent in Saskatchewan; and, as I said earlier, by almost 200 per cent in British Columbia. Clearly, much has been done in the past, but much more remains to be done.
Hon. members, I am sure, are aware of the commitments which the government made in the Speech from the Throne. I draw to their attention again the belief of the government as expressed in these words:
-that a better balance should be established between the money spent to introduce bilingualism in the public service and the money spent to enable more Canadians, particularly young people, to learn to communicate in both official languages.
That does not mean we must diminish our efforts to improve the bilingual capacity of our civil service. It means we must do more to extend our efforts to younger Canadians.
-the government intends to discuss with the provinces arrangements to increase the effectiveness of training in both official languages in the school systems across Canada.
I am sure the provinces will welcome our desire to be helpful in this area and I am sure we shall receive their full co-operation. I would not want hon. members to have exaggerated expectations about what can be done immediately. The limitations are not necessarily financial; there are limitations of human resources. We cannot, with a wave of a magic wand, increase these services and extend them immediately to every point where it is desirable to have them. But that is the kind of effort we intend to make in the very near future.

I must say that, however important it may be to put the accent on expanding our youth programs, this entails no reduction in our support for institutional bilingualism. It is very important in our view, not only in substance, but also for symbolic reasons.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal) who spoke Wednesday, underlined the fact there is still a lack of francophones at the executive level in a number of departments. We have not yet reached the point where there are equal numbers of francophones and anglophones in the public service. It is no easy thing either to tell francophones, after 110 years of confederation, that equal opportunities in the public service are always for tomorrow, never for today. It is important however to maintain our efforts for a bilingual public service in Canada.

There can be no wavering, although we may find more effective ways of doing it. We may be able to save money and stop the wastage of money. But on the commitment of ensuring that French-speaking Canadians have equal opportunity within the civil service, and that we should expand our ability to serve the public in both official languages, there can be no diminution and no pulling back.
The Address-Mr. Roberts
[ Translation]
I must also say a few words concerning the situation of francophones outside Quebec. Bilingualism is not a policy directed to Quebec francophones only it is also for Frenchspeaking Canadians outside Quebec.
Yesterday I noted, as I hope this House did also the remarks by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). It is important in my view for us in government to give our support to the French-speaking community outside Quebec, to be sure to protect them against assimilation. It is not only a question of giving education safeguards, nor giving TV access to culture. It is important to try and maintain a French language context in those communities, in order one may live in one's official language, albeit a minority one. It is also important to guarantee that not only for the benefit of francophones outside Quebec, but also for anglophones within Quebec.
If I could put this policy which I have just described in a larger context, I would describe it as one of our many policies directed toward overcoming divisions in Canada and bringing us together. Language rights are not the only problem in Canada. It is an important problem, but not the only one. Many people in the Atlantic provinces are perhaps more concerned about the problem of lagging economic development. Many people in western Canada are concerned about their sense of alienation or isolation from the decision-making centres of eastern Canada.
There are a variety of problems which face this country. We have developed programs, sometimes successfully but not always, which try to overcome regional disparities in this country. We think it is important that the Atlantic provinces be given equality of economic opportunity to that which exists in other parts of the country. We have tried to develop policies, perhaps not always successfully, which take into account the concerns of citizens of the western provinces. We have tried to develop a transportation policy which provides equality of access to communication and transportation in this country. We have tried to design these policies to overcome barriers between Canadians. They have been designed to bring Canadians together. Therefore, our language policy must enable Canadians to come together. All Canadians should be allowed fully to live with their language without being in the position of second-class citizens.
Our official languages policy helps to protect fundamental human rights. It attempts to overcome divisions which would otherwise lead to explosive grievances based on real injustice. It is on that point I would like to repeat my earlier comments on the remarks of the former minister of national defence, a man whom I respect greatly, a man who is extremely sincere in the statements he makes, a man who perhaps reflects the feelings of other Canadians. However, I say to him that the official languages policy is not something that creates divisions in this country. It is something which helps us to overcome these divisions. That is its real importance of the policy. Our

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. Roberts
official languages policy enables us to try to overcome what would otherwise be real grievances and bitter frustrations over the situation of languages in this country. It is in that context we should perceive our policy of official languages.
I have discussed our official languages policy thus far in terms of the protection of rights. I would like briefly to discuss one or two other aspects. I suggest that a policy of protection of our official languages creates the kind of structure in which a multicultural society can thrive. It is trite to say that in the United States they have a different idea of their country, one which is an assimilation or melting-pot. That is what a melting-pot is, an assimilation. The protection of our two official languages establishes a basic structure which accepts and encourages the importance of diversity of cultural point of view. I suggest that a bilingual country, in the sense of having language rights, is one which would be more open and tolerant with regard to a variety of cultural expression, something which makes Canada a distinctive and valuable place in which to live. It helps strengthen our unique multicultural society.
We do not look upon the acceptance of these two major international languages in Canada as a problem or limitation, but as a splendid opportunity.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: On language rights it often seems that Canadians are like the man running along, who stumbled on an opportunity and picked himself up, dusted himself off and ran unheeding on his way as quickly as he could. The existence in Canada of these two major languages-the only developed country to have them-provides us with an economic resource. We should look at the advantages they bring to Canada as a trading nation in the decade to come, and realize the potential of the English-speaking market to the south and the Common Market in which the two major languages are English and French. The language facility that we have is a great advantage; it is an opportunity to be exploited, not a fact to be condemned.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the intervention of the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) because I wish to speak for a few minutes on the bilingual issue. It is one which is shaking the foundations of our country. Nothing I shall say today has not already been written in the Toronto Star in the last few days.
When a western minister, one of the few from western Canada, resigns because bilingualism is too encompassing, and when on the other hand, another cabinet minister leaves to join the provincial political field in Quebec because bilingualism is applied too easily, it seems time to inquire whether or not the policy was fundamentally in error from the start. Yet the bases of bilingualism are not being examined or debated at the national political level, despite the enormous groundswell of popular opposition and the indifference of French Canadians in Quebec. A policy which arouses only mild enthusiasm among the minority it proposes to help, while giving rise to intense hostility among the majority, deserves careful scrutiny. Yet political parties have been unable to carry out any examination of the principle of bilingualism.
The government blames the backlash which has developed in English-speaking Canada on bigotry or red-necked racism. I do not believe this is justified. In my view, Anglophone Canada can be considered one of the more tolerant societies in the world. After all, every society has its own expressions of intolerance. There are plenty of irritants around. But if one examines the causes carefully, one finds that the principle of bilingualism is offending many people.
Inherent in that principle is the assumption that there are two founding races in Canada and that these two founding races occupy, somehow, an elitist position compared with other races. No account is taken of the fact that the Indians were here long before either of the two founding races arrived. Then, again, in my riding many people who came from eastern Europe would consider themselves a founding race because they were the ones who cleared the forests in that area and made a productive part of Canada out of the wilderness.
All these so-called ethnic groups lived through a period in which they were not accepted as first-class citizens in Englishspeaking Canada. Today, we seem to have adopted a founding race concept which belittles those whose original language was neither English nor French, marking them as somehow different. The idea that there is one founding race, let alone two, makes it difficult to apply the concept of equality in a democratic and fairly egalitarian country. It seems important to me that the idea of equal opportunity should seem to be real, even if its application is not always possible.
During the original debate on bilingualism in 1969, I made the point that the civil service should represent the regionalism which is a fact of life in this country. It is of little help to have a civil servant who speaks both languages but who is totally ignorant of the part of the country he administers. As a western Canadian, it has been my experience that many of the
The Address-Mr. Ritchie
civil servants with whom I have been in contact have no concept of the nature of our problems in the west.
The idea behind bilingualism was to help those Canadians whose mother tongue was French but who did not hold nearly their share of the total civil service jobs available. Today, English-speaking Canadians fear compulsory bilingualism will bar them from the top positions in national politics and the public service. Nor can their fears be dismissed as groundless.
I might mention the joke about the lifeguard from Victoria who eventually managed to get a job at 24 Sussex Drive because, although he could not swim, he was bilingual.
I am indebted to a columnist, Mr. Robert Nielsen, for some interesting figures which appeared in yesterday's Star. He drew attention to some pertinent statistics derived from the 1971 census. The census found that 14,470,000 Canadians speak English only, that 3,879,000 speak French only, and that
2,900,000	speak both languages. It also found that the language most often used at home was English for 14,446,000 people, French for 5,546,000, and some other tongue approximately 1,600,000.
From these figures it can be inferred that Francophones comprise about 1.7 million of the nearly 3 million Canadians who speak both French and English, or 60 per cent. Thus, they have a 60 per cent start when it comes to filling the bilingual jobs in the federal civil service and in Crown corporations such as Air Canada or the CBC, although they comprise only 26 per cent of the population. In other words, a French-Canadian has four times the chance of getting a job in the senior civil service, compared with a Canadian who grows up in an English-speaking home.
When one considers that all federal supervisory jobs are scheduled to be bilingual by 1978, it is evident that French-Canadians have an inside start, especially since it is not easy to train adults to become proficient in a second language, as we have all observed, judging by the problems which have beset the federal government's language training program. Perhaps the disadvantage suffered by English-speaking Canadians is even greater than the figures I have quoted suggest, since many of the uniligual English speakers live in British Columbia or the maritimes, and the farther away one lives from the seat of government, the less chance exists of getting into the civil service. This is a fact of geography and I am not suggesting that any one person is to blame for it.
Western Canadians, in particular, point out that though they are able to join the civil service, the RCMP and the armed forces, application of the bilingual principle makes it impossible for a great many of them to occupy positions of seniority. Mr. Speaker, when the majority of the country feels dissatisfied and disadvantaged in the competition for jobs in the civil service, the armed forces or the RCMP, it surely spells great trouble for us all.
What about the minority which bilingualism was supposed to help? The program may have made it much easier for French Canadians to take jobs in the civil service-indeed, I believe it has done so-but has it accomplished its goal of swinging their loyalty from the province of Quebec to Canada

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. Ritchie

But it would appear that French Canadians are building their defences in Quebec through Bill 22 which establishes French as the official language in the province. I can understand the purpose of Bill 22, but it is extremely difficult to suggest that it is in keeping with the principles of the Official Languages Act, which itself imposes an unwanted degree of bilingualism on the rest of the country.
[DOT] (M50)
Political writers and thinking Canadians, particularly western Canadians, are wondering where all this is going to lead. Will it lead to the break-up of the country? Writing in the Toronto Star of October 12, 1976, Richard Gwyn suggested that the "two nations" idea is once again respectable. Bilingualism, which was to be the government's response to the problem, has proved to be a cure as powerful as the original disease. Perhaps it is bigotry, perhaps it is unwarranted fear, but the concept of support for bilingualism has collapsed in English Canada today. Even the premiers of the provinces seemed to be heading toward a form of two nations when they agreed in Toronto that they should have an expansion of jurisdiction over culture, communications and immigration. If a province can have control over immigration, control over who shall enter or leave the province, then in effect it is largely an independent state.
It seems to me that the English-speaking premiers realized that only the province of Quebec would tug away jurisdiction in the fields of culture, communications and immigration. Surely this is "two nations by the back door", whether you want to call it that or not. Many English Canadians have already, unfortunately, separated themselves from the province of Quebec, and certainly this is very true of western Canadians. On the other hand, in Quebec Mr. Bourassa seems to have gained popular support for Bill 22.
Will confederation return to the two nations concept? I do not know. I believe that bilingualism, without some modification of the present policy, has ceased to be practical. The idea in the throne speech of more education in both languages might be helpful, but that is far into the future. Many of us who went to school did have some opportunity to learn a second language. Perhaps the teaching standards in those days were poor compared to the standards of today, but in many instances a kind of resentment was built up.
I should also like to mention a program referred to by the Secretary of State, the aim of which is to transport our youth from one part of the country to another for educational purposes. I know one instance where this worked in reverse In my riding, a certain school band conceived the idea of going to Scotland to compete in a music festival. They made great efforts to apply many times to the Secretary of State for a grant, but found no grants were available. Therefore, the children and parents had to pay their own way, raising $640 apiece. While in Scotland they met a group from Quebec, students of approximately the same age and attending the

same kind of school. These students had had their way paid. So in this instance the program worked in reverse.
I know of another instance where a school band made a visit to Holland to play at one of the towns that the Canadians had liberated during the war. They were royally received by the burgomaster and given a town banquet. Then the external affairs people swarmed around them and said what a great thing it was for Canada that they had made the trip. In their opinion, this was only adding insult to injury.
The resignation of the former minister of national defence and the response to his going has certainly indicated that there are large numbers of western Canadians, at least, who view the present bilingualism program as unworkable. There is no evidence in the throne speech that the government intends to modify or to change in any way the workings of this program. This, as much as anything, is aggrieving the Canadian public, and the government, unfortunately, has indicated no real initiatives to deal with this vexing problem.

Yes, another subsidy. The government said in the throne speech that the "international trading environment will profoundly affect our economic performance". Indeed it will, Mr. Speaker. The fact of the matter is that the economy of Canada is resource-based and the bulk of our exports, approximately 71 per cent, is raw materials. Our major trading partners are very happy with the situation. A perfect example of this is our relationship with Japan. We have a trade surplus with that country, yet they are quite happy. They are happy because only 3 per cent or 4 per cent of the goods we export to Japan are manufactured goods, whereas their total exports to Canada consist of manufactured products such as electronic equipment, cars and cameras. Inherent in that trade surplus is the number of jobs created by manufacturing from Canadian raw materials. No wonder they are happy with the situation and do not want it changed.
Coupled with that is the growing mechanization of the resource sector of the economy, resulting in greater productivity with fewer hands required. We have a prime example of that situation in northern Ontario where our economy is resource-based. In fact, we are losing our population, as this House well knows, and as a result of that loss of population we will lose one of our federal seats in this House.
(Mr. Rodriguez.]
It is absolutely important that we realize where the problem lies. The development of selling resources and buying back finished products is not accidental. In the past, these resources were handy and appeared to be inexhaustible. The pick-up artists in the business community and in government, federal and provincial, exploited them for all they were worth, all the time locking us into a long-term pattern of development which is so startlingly dramatized by our trade relations with Japan.
The pattern has a certain vicious life of its own. In trying to balance the dollar value of imports with the dollar value of exports, we must sell more and more of our resources. Because these resources are not handy any more, vast sums of capital must be found to explore and develop them. It is on this point that the mining corporations in Canada have replaced the banks as the worst bitchers in the country. It is part of the pattern that they now howl for government to give them more, and greater tax concessions to further the pattern in which we are hewers of wood and drawers of water.
The Liberal government is not prepared to tackle this problem because it means taking on the corporate elite of this country, the Steven Romans, the Zimmermans, the Grubs, and so on, where the power of the boardroom decides the fate of governments. I mentioned Roman. He is a Tory. He used to be a Liberal. Now he is trying to be on both sides of the fence. That is the reason the throne speech avoids facing this problem like the plague. Instead, the government talks about training Canadians for non-existent jobs. The government, instead of dealing with the problem, comes up with band-aid solutions such as this throne speech talks about. Equally laughable, in spite of the seriousness of our predicament, is this gem from the throne speech:
In pursuit of the goal of a higher rate of employment it will be necessary to improve the efficiency of the labour market and actively hasten the return of the unemployed to productive labour.
There has been a conspiracy in this country in the last year and a half among government and its cohorts in the boardrooms across the nation: they entered into a conspiracy to find a scapegoat for the mismanagement of the country. Together, they concocted a mythology about the Canadian labour force, and in co-operation with their media arm they propagandized the public. Here is the scenario from their combined points of view: Canadian workers are less productive than their United States brothers and sisters, yet want more pay for less productivity. Furthermore, Canadian trade unions are too powerful and are primarily responsible for the high inflation rate in Canada.
It is time this unholy alliance was unmasked. It is time for us to look at that mythology, to look at that lie which has been propagated for the benefit of protecting this government. We should look at some of the recently released and corrected figures regarding productivity between Canada and the United States which reveal that between 1969 and 1974 the annual productivity rate in the U.S. was 1.9 per cent, whereas in Canada it was 2.8 per cent. It led one bank economist to declare that Canadian wages have risen more rapidly in the

This government has a leadership role to play in making sure that comes about. They must not let the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) dilly-dally and shilly-shally and sit on the fence on this issue. Let me say a few words, Mr. Speaker, with respect to the recent demonstration by labour against the government's so-called wage and price controls program. Let us not forget that the Conservatives proposed such a program in 1974 and the Liberal Party of Canada ran their election opposing it. As a matter of fact, I happen to have one of the campaign leaflets of the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Faulkner), who has just been demoted from Secretary of State to Minister of Science and Technology. I want to read from it. On the inside is a picture of the hon. member, minus his beard, and headlined beside it, "Wage and price controls ... What's wrong with them". The text reads:
Wage and price controls are an administrative monster-once born it grows like a cancer and is impossible to stop.
Wage and price controls cause shortages.
Wage and price controls misguide the public. They draw attention away from those factors which do affect inflation-productivity, supply and demand, rising importations, tax rates, energy costs, etc.

Think about it? Avoid wage and price controls! Vote Liberal. Vote Faulkner.

To keep their freedom it was absolutely incumbent on Canadians to protest last Thursday by the most serious, non-violent means possible. I supported that protest, and suggest to those who talk about broken contracts and illegalities that they ought to consider seriously that it is in the face of a sheepish citizenry that despotism breeds and thrives, that when a government lies to its citizens it has broken faith with them and it ought not to expect anything less than the most vigorous response.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in the debate on the Speech from the Throne outlining the federal government's legislative program for the second session of the thirtieth parliament of Canada, I should like to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne for their very thoughtful and constructive contribution to this debate.
I also wish to congratulate you, sir, on your appointment and also to express my congratulations to the newly appointed ministers, parliamentary secretaries and other officers on their appointments. I offer them my co-operation and wish them success in carrying out their duties for the greater good of Canadians in all parts of Canada.
I truly believe that the present session of parliament is shaping up into the most important and, indeed, most crucial session of our parliamentary career. At least, I believe it is so in my case since I was first elected to the House in 1957. At this moment in our history, each and every one of us should avoid intemperate words and shallow remarks, and instead offer our sincere and best advice to the government which is challenged today by serious economic and social problems threatening the survival of our country. We should be positive at all times in our response to the government's comprehensive program which was designed to strengthen national unity and improve the quality of life for all Canadians, to build a harmonious society and a united country which will better fulfil the needs and aspirations of our people.
Along with many members of the House, I welcome in particular those initiatives announced in the Speech from the Throne which are evidence of the federal government's determination to give enlightened leadership, strong government and unwavering confidence to the Canadian people who are impatiently awaiting our best efforts in these difficult times. The Canadian people today want to be fully and clearly informed about the future. This is, therefore, not the time for half-measures, hesitation or petty politics. Already there has been too much rhetoric and hot air in this House and outside of it on many national issues. It is time we dealt with the big problems, especially those of inflation and the high rate of unemployment.
In dealing with inflation, the government found it necessary in October of 1975 to introduce a temporary program of direct control of incomes and prices. During the past year, most Canadians have co-operated with the government to restrain their demands on the economy, and as a result the inflation psychosis which gripped many Canadians has subsided.
I am also very happy that the provincial governments signed an agreement with the federal government and joined us in this national effort to control the dread disease of inflation. That is why today we are relieved to learn that the cost of living or the consumer price index, rose at a significantly lower rate during the past year than the year before. The true fact is that the consumer price index rose at the rate of 10.6 per cent in October, 1975, and last month it had dropped to 6.5 per
October 21, 1976

cent. This has benefited everyone in Canada, particularly those on low incomes. The fact is that the increase in the cost living is declining and that Canadian workers, under the anti-inflation guidelines, have been allowed increases in income greater than the increase in the cost of living.
This real gain in income of approximately 4 per cent over the last year has also increased our purchasing power. The anti-inflation program is working and that is why, as we enter the second year of the program, Canadians can expect a further reduction in the rate of inflation. I agree with those Canadians who advocate the removal of controls sometime in 1977, however, because the main advantages of the program are being achieved and it is rough justice which I do not believe can be tolerated too long. We, therefore, welcome the discussion and studies undertaken to lay the groundwork for the removal of controls without the renewal of inflation. Such objectives will be more easily achieved by the government's announcement to limit the rate of growth in government spending. The Bank of Canada's decision to reduce the rate of money supply will also help to contain inflation.
I believe that in these days public sector employer-employee relations should be regarded as an essential element in fighting inflation. Along with improved labour-management relations in the private sector, and measures to increase productivity, the post-controls strategy should study the effect of high interest rates on the consumer as well as on business expansion. I believe that the present high interest rates on loans for business expansion, especially the high interest rates on first and second mortgages, are a deterrent to an increase in the economy, and add to inflation.
I receive many representations from the people in Parkdale, Mr. Speaker, and I believe that other members of the House receive similar representations, to the effect that the money supply policies in Canada must be reviewed. The current high interest rates of 3 per cent to 4 percentage points more than in the United States are costly; they prohibit business expansion and in many cases reduce the ability of Canadians to buy their own homes. High interest rates for first and second mortgages definitely contribute to the difficulty of acquiring a house, especially for a workingman who wishes his family to live quietly and peacefully rather than be closed in a high-rise apartment building.
At the same time, agencies like the government's foreign investment review agency should extend their activities to not only preserve but also produce more jobs for Canadians. In the final analysis, the responsibility for decisions about the right kind of strategy for the post-controls period will rest on the shoulders of the government and parliament, which will be asked to approve the new programs. In this process, however, all sectors of the Canadian economy should be consulted.
In this process of consultation we are happy to learn that labour will not be forgotten. The Speech from the Throne announced measures to improve labour-management relations in Canada. I believe there is complete agreement that improvements in the collective bargaining system are urgently needed to avoid so many costly strikes, loss of productivity and
The Address-Mr. Haidasz
increased social unrest. We, therefore, welcome the initiatives of our government to establish a collective bargaining centre and encourage greater participation by plant workers in decisions affecting their working conditions, upgrading of skills and job safety, with security and adequate pensions.
In particular, I enthusiastically approve the federal government's decision to establish an industrial safety and health centre to assist both companies and workers to identify and remove hazards. I hope that all provincial governments will follow the leadership of the federal government and to do their share in their respective fields of responsibility.
Industrialization and swiftly increasing technology, with its resultant new products, are radically altering the environment and exposing man to growing amounts of harmful pollutants and dangerous products. Today we are faced with the great problem of environmental diseases which were unknown 30 years ago. Among these environmental diseases we include cancer caused by various chemicals and substances such as asbestos, vinyl chloride and even chlorinated water when combined with certain pollutants. Other environmental diseases include birth defects, mercury poisoning, respiratory disorders, and deafness. The proposed industrial safety and health centre should be able to identify health hazards quickly and recommend changes and strict enforcement of regulations, or help establish new regulations and prevent new toxic substances from entering the environment by adequate testing and screening out dangerous chemical compounds before they are used in products or manufacturing processes.
I believe that the federal government should give serious consideration to special toxic substances' regulations, making it the responsibility of manufacturers to prove that all their products are safe before they are put on the market. This national industrial safety and health centre should also deal without delay with industrial noise which is causing occupational hearing loss, now the third most common industrial disease in Ontario. Mr. Speaker, deafness is a silent, invisible, painless epidemic which today afflicts more Canadians than are sick from cancer, venereal disease, blindness and multiple sclerosis put together.
As a physician, I greet with satisfaction the initiative of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to tackle the problem of alcohol abuse which is costing our economy about $1 million every day but is, above all, causing untold harm to personal and family life and contributing to
3,000	deaths in road accidents. It is costing the country $360 million every year in health and hospital expenses. Alcoholic cirrhosis of the liver, a complication of alcoholism and a leading cause of death among heavy drinkers, has become the fastest rising killer in the over-25 age group in Canada, thus putting this disease ahead of lung cancer and suicide.
I am disappointed, however, that no substantial effort has been made to fight the ravages of heart disease and arteriosclerotic complications, the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in Canada, which has reached epidemic proportions. I urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare to organize a concerted campaign to fight this crippling disease.

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. Haidasz
The bulk of representations made in my constituency office consists of representations for adequate housing at affordable prices. Adequate accommodation at affordable prices is necessary to a stable society. The ownership of a home for his wife and children is the goal of the workingman, or of most workingmen. He would sooner own a home than be squeezed into a tight and crowded apartment building. It is, therefore, particularly important to provide this much needed shelter at a reasonable price. Unfortunately, the relatively cheap mortgage money under the federal government's Assisted Home Ownership Plan is only available to those whose monthly payments are not more than 25 per cent of their total income. This means that because of the great increase in the price of houses, less than 30 per cent of Ontario families in 1974 were eligible for this program. Therefore, other programs should be devised to meet the needs of the majority of our population.
I believe present mortgage interest rates of 12 per cent are too high, and the required down payment is beyond the capacity of many people. Surely, more could be done, indeed must be done, in a country as rich as Canada to reach the desirable social goal of home ownership. Surely, government at various levels could help eliminate some of the barriers to home ownership, such as the high price of land. We need less red tape in the approval of developments and provision of serviced land, a simplified and unified building code, lower charges for registration, reduced costs for developers, builders and buyers and, especially, mortgage rates at reasonable levels. In a just society we should strive to provide a decent house at a reasonable cost for the workingman.
We also welcome the federal government's new campaign to assist small business by appointing a special minister of state to develop better programs for this important sector of our economy. The proposed assistance in reducing paper work, providing easier and larger loans and more consulting services, will strengthen the position of small business and provide more jobs and greater economic growth. Moreover, as Canadian subsidiaries of large foreign corporations have great advantages over their Canadian competitors, some tax advantages or incentives should be forthcoming to Canadian-controlled companies.
Many Canadians are impatiently awaiting either a new or a thoroughly revised Immigration Act. Modern Canada is a country of immigrants or descendants of immigrants, shared with Canadian Indians and the Inuit people. Therefore a just, sound and farsighted immigration policy, administered under a new Immigration Act, would contribute immensely to greater national development, family unity and the cultural enrichment of our country.
No Speech from the Throne includes all the proposed legislation the government intends to bring before parliament. I therefore urge the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) to reintroduce the legislation knows as Bill C-83 in the previous session, an act for the better protection of Canadian society against perpetrators of violent crime. Many members con-

sidered this legislation a necessary precondition to the legislation amending the Criminal Code with respect to murder.
In view of the make-up and nature of the population of my constituency, Parkdale, I am greatly interested in the proposed legislation on human rights. The purpose of this legislation is to prohibit discrimination on the grounds of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion, age, sex, marital status or physical handicap.
