In particular, the human rights bill will establish the principle of equal compensation for work of equal value performed by persons of either sex. It will also establish a citizen's statutory right to gain greater access to personal records in federal information files and to correct that information when it is in error.
I urge the Minister of Justice to review the bill he brought forward in the last parliament. I urge him especially to make a study of the unfair sections and bad effects of Quebec's official language act, often referred to as Bill 22. Along with many Canadians, I am not in accord with some of the principles embodied in the act, in particular the one restricting the freedom of parents to choose the language of education for their children. It is contrary to the letter of the Canadian charter of human rights which our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), when he was Minister of Justice, presented to a federal-provincial constitutional conference in January, 1968.1 wish to draw the attention of hon. members to that charter, especially page 27. As for education it speaks of
-guaranteeing the right of the individual to education in institutions using as a medium of instruction the official language of his choice.
Bill 22 also appears to go against the spirit of international declarations and covenants on human rights which Canada has ratified.
I welcome the Prime Minister's commitment, as set out in the Speech from the Throne, that grievances from public servants through the Commissioner of Official Languages will continue to be reviewed and that the government will ensure maximum fairness and effectiveness in the implementation of the official languages policy, especially in finding a better way of spending taxpayers' money, by introducing bilingualism in our schools. I am sure we all agree that the great majority of Canadians are dedicated to the strengthening of bonds between Canadians speaking our two official languages and those belonging to our many different cultures. I firmly believe that multi-culturalism can only thrive within the framework and harmonious atmosphere of official bilingualism.
We must not allow fear, prejudice, misinformation or discrimination to dominate our reason and passion. We must, rather, display tolerance and understanding; otherwise all Canadians would lose, and all Canada would be lost, this great country, the envy of the world, which our predecessors built up and left to us in trust-a country which it is our moral duty to pass on to future generations, strong and united.
October 21, 1976

Mr. Speaker, may I continue? I join with others in extending my sincere compliments to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I would also like to compliment my leader for his effective and worthwhile comments last week in this debate. Perhaps I should make no comment about the contribution of the Prime Minister. Why embarrass his followers any further?
I rise today to address this House on matters of great concern to me. I refer to the fragile state of our economy and the continuing deception and duplicity on the part of the government by their omission or commission on issues vitally important to this country. The Prime Minister, in his remarks to this House, devoted considerable time to defending his administration's wage and price controls program. It was difficult for him to claim any victory, however, without twisting the cost of living figures a wee bit. That, I suggest, is exactly what he did. What he did not do, at least to any real extent, was address himself to this nation's worsening position in foreign trade, our rising unemployment and our net real growth.
Let me begin by noting a few conspicuous distortions in the Prime Minister's remarks on the controls program, and briefly mention what the government has failed to tell us about Canada's place in the world markets. Sitting in Canada, unless you travel or wish to invest in a foreign country, it is often difficult to realize that we are literally sinking as a nation as far as our dollar's buying power is concerned in relation to many other nations of the world. Sure, we are very rightfully, disturbed about regional differences in Canada, and I suggest that more and more people agree that such regional differences should be eliminated as far as possible. However, are we really achieving something worth while if we allow the nation in general to sink lower and lower in terms of our real worth and value in relation to other nations?
When this government initially took office, we were proud number two among the world's nations as far as per capita income was concerned; close to being number one, number one being the United States. Where are we today? We are number seven. The Americans have held their position at number one,
The Address-Mr. Stevens
but under this administration we have sunk to seventh in the world. When we deal with this topic, I draw hon. members' attention to the fact that two years ago the government spoke of the relationship of inflation here at home to international conditions abroad. In that Speech from the Throne in September, 1974, we recall how they painted a picture that somehow we had become tangled up in world conditions, that inflation was an international phenomenon and that somehow we in Canada would have to wait until that phenomenon changed internationally before we could do much about it in this country.
It is very interesting to note, if you read that throne speech, that the government very clearly predicted that international food and commodity prices would fall and return to what they called a normal level. That was the message two years ago. However, rather than take the crest out of the inflation that they anticipated with a controls program that could have been instituted in July, 1974-and, incidentally, as was suggested at that time by my party-this government chose to wait. The government waited a full year before they instituted a controls program. I suggest they instituted it at the wrong time and have delivered an administrative monstrosity in their program.
Strangely enough, we sat in this very chamber and listened to the Prime Minister now attempt to take credit for the fall-off in prices that only two years ago they predicted in their throne speech was going to occur. He takes credit because he is trying desperately to justify the controls program that was instituted in his own caucus and in this House on the people of Canada.
Much has been made in this House and elsewhere of the fact that the annual rate of change in consumer prices fell from 10.6 per cent in October, 1975, to 6.5 per cent in September, 1976. However, almost all this improvement resulted from the decline in food prices. It is the farmer who has taken the brunt of the government's anti-inflation program, yet it is the government that is now attempting to take the credit for any fall-off in prices that we are now experiencing. Let me be specific.

I have been asked to explain myself, and I will do exactly that. I ask the hon. member to quieten down and listen to a few figures. The annual rate of increase in food prices decelerated from 12 per cent at the start of the controls program to a negative 15 per cent in September, 1976. That is how the farmer is being hurt by this Trudeau administration. Remember, food prices are only affected in an indirect way by the anti-inflation program. The area of consumer expenditures more directly affected by the controls program, non-food items, has shown only a minor improvement, decelerating from 10.2 per cent in October to only 9.3 per cent in September, 1976. The claim that the consumer price index figures show inflation to be under control is more than just premature; it is sheer nonsense. Clearly, the government is trying to declare

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. Stevens
victory in the fight against inflation on the basis of faulty statistics.
The government argues that lower agricultural prices have been passed on to the consumer because the profit margins of distributors, processors and retailers are controlled even though food prices at the farm gate are not. Hon. members will recall that in addressing this House, both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) made this point quite clear. I wish to read into the record what the Prime Minister stated on October 13 as reported at page 31 of Hansard:
-what is important to the worker's wife when she goes shopping is that, because of price controls, she has more purchasing power this year than she had in 1975 before controls. Apparently it does not suit the CLC or the NDP, or for that matter the Tories, to tell that to the Canadian worker and to his wife. I wonder why. Perhaps the opposition will tell us why during the course of this debate-
I welcome that invitation by the Prime Minister. The truthful answer is that his Figures are dead wrong. They are dead wrong according to the figures of October 12 by the Department of Finance. Before getting to those figures, I want to show what the Minister of Finance stated, as well as indicate that the Prime Minister went on to say that 60 per cent of the cost of food was made up of such items as distribution costs, profits and other related matters. In the same debate, on October 14, the Minister of Finance said the following:
-as a result of the work of the Food Prices Review Board, and what now seems to be forgotten, is that up to 60 per cent of the cost which the consumer pays for his food arises from the costs of transportation, processing and distribution of food products.
That is the figure. Let us remember it. The Prime Minister said it was about 60 per cent. The Minister of Finance was a little more honest. He said "up to 60 per cent". What are the actual facts disclosed by the Minister of Finance in his own paper which he tabled, entitled "Status report, the anti-inflation program and the economy". I refer to the first page, wherein it is stated:
Depending on the item, from 30 per cent to 55 per cent of the price the consumer pays for food is accounted for by transportation, processing and distribution activities which are controlled under the anti-inflation program.
I have never seen such a contradiction, in one week, between a statement made by the Minister of Finance, earlier by the Prime Minister, and then refuted by the very paper which the Minister of Finance had previously submitted to the House. Our consumer price index is made up of many items in different categories, but about 30 per cent relates to food and, as we know, food prices at the farm gate are not controlled. Yet this is the area in which the sharpest decline has taken place. Nowhere has this administration thanked the farmer for allowing prices to fall as a result of market action-by as much as 20 per cent in the case of beef. Nowhere has the administration singled out those who are the chief inflation fighters in Canada, namely, our farmers. Nowhere does the administration give any credit to the marketplace as being the chief ingredient in lowering prices in this country. There is no mention of that truth.

There is no mention of another observation made in the paper to which I have referred. At the present time, a vicious price war is going on among the grocery chains, and any suggestion that they are abiding by the anti-inflation program is not true. In some cases they are running their businesses at sharp losses, which means that food prices are lower than they might otherwise be. But the situation I have described will not last and prices, as far as the food element is concerned, will begin to increase. Let us not allow the administration to say prematurely that somehow controls are having an effect on prices. That has not been demonstrated.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that I prefaced my remarks by commenting on the government's duplicity with regard to issues vital to the well-being of this country. Another example of such duplicity is the flip-flop during the election campaign. You will recall that the Liberal party energetically campaigned against wage-freezing and price controls. They went from riding to riding stating that such a program would be detrimental to the economy. Yet little more than a year later, without a mandate, they brought in the very controls against which they had campaigned.
The Prime Minister stated in his speech that inflation was down to 6.5 per cent. But look at the facts. Even if the administration succeeds in reaching the goal of 4 per cent, what will it have achieved? It will have brought the level of inflation back to where it was in 1971. Isn't it ludicrous to create a problem through irresponsible monetary and fiscal policies and then expect this House and the people of Canada to congratulate the government for returning the nation, as far as inflation in concerned, to the state it was in in 1971 when most of the problem arose? I have already referred to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Finance, but perhaps in all fairness I should not dwell exclusively on those two-

speechtext: "Characters."

speechtext:
However, I should point out, in all fairness to the Prime Minister, that the record seems to deteriorate from the time John Turner took over as minister of finance in January, 1972. When he took over from Edgar Benson, inflation was running at 4.9 per cent. When he left, it was 10.6 per cent. During his 44 months in office, the cost of living jumped by 38.5 per cent and the dollar, if one assumes it to be worth 100 cents in January, 1972, was worth only 72 cents when he walked out.
At the time John Turner was given the mantle in January, 1972, there were 544,000 people out of work. When he left,
732,000	were unemployed. In spite of all his huffing and puffing, in spite of all the measures he took to facilitate employment in business, only 69,000 jobs were created in the manufacturing sector from December, 1971 to December,
1975.	In 1972 there was a surplus of $700 million in our current account balance. In 1975 there was a deficit of almost $5 billion. In the aggregate, since John Turner took over, the nation has had a current account deficit every year. Including the projections for 1976-a deficit estimated at $4.5 billion-
October 21, 1976

our current account balances will have aggregated approximately $11 billion in the red.
To put it another way, last year and this year Canada will have the largest current account deficit of any country in the world. So let us not laugh at Great Britain, or at Italy or at other countries which have deficits until we have taken a good look at ourselves. Consider Britain, for example, a country almost totally lacking in natural resources such as Canada has exploited for so long. Is it not remarkable that we should be running a greater current account deficit than that nation, despite all its troubles?
This is a situation which the administration must take to heart. It is one which must be challenged and reversed. But let me get back to our wonder boy, John Turner. Frankly, the biggest wonder about John Turner is that he was allowed to stay on for as long as he did. When he got the job as minister of finance, real growth in this country amounted to 6.6 per cent. When he left, it was .3 per cent and on a per capita basis it was negative. In terms of real growth, the ground we lost under John Turner as minister of finance now costs this country $5 billion a year, or almost $200 per person. In addition, there are some 200,000 more people out of work as a further consequence.
Consider the record with regard to federal government restraint. During the period in which Turner was minister of finance, spending by the federal government jumped 99.8 per cent. To put it in another way, it took us 105 years to reach a federal spending level of $17,004,400,000. John Turner doubled that figure in 44 months. In the aggregate, Mr. Speaker, under the budgets that he brought into the House, $113 billion of taxpayers' money was spent, or at least borrowed. Is it not sheer hypocrisy that the same John Turner now righteously speaks at various club meetings about excessive government spending?
What did he do about excessive government spending when he was in office and could do something about it? The fact is that he ran. Since the time that he ran, he has not even had the courtesy to tell the House or the people of Canada why he ran. At least the most recent ex-minister, the former minister of national defence, has attempted to explain to the Canadian public the reason for his defection from the cabinet. Not so the former minister of finance. We thought that Edgar Benson was bad, Mr. Speaker. In fact, many things about Benson appeared to be undesirable so far as his handling of the finance portfolio was concerned. But let me assure the House that compared with John Turner's spending habits, Benson was a Scrooge.
However, there is some hope, Mr. Speaker. We now have a new Minister of Finance, a man who we all know hopes to be prime minister. In fact, I understand that is the main reason he took the job of Minister of Finance. He is prime minister-in-waiting, if you like. Meanwhile, we in the nation have to wait for some economic policy. Perhaps it is too early to judge the record of the Minister of Finance, though to date that
The Address*-Mr. Stevens
record seems to be one of lurching from indecision to indecision. As we know, the Minister of Finance has tabled a working paper entitled "The Way Ahead", obviously looking for a program for the post-controls period.
As an old Osgoode Hall classmate of the minister, may I suggest that it is not necessarily innovation that is needed to solve our problems, but primarily a policy that gets back to some sound fundamentals, to some basics in terms of fiscal and monetary matters. If the minister does not want to take Conservative precedents, let him look at the government of Louis St. Laurent and the then finance minister, Walter Harris. I say that because it is of interest to note that in the year 1955, the year the minister of finance and I graduated from Osgoode Hall, inflation in this country was one-tenth of 1 per cent, real growth was 10 per cent and unemployment was 4.4 per cent.
In the interval, the figures for real growth and inflation have just about been reversed. We have ended up with 10 per cent inflation, rather than 10 per cent real growth; we are in a position where we had virtually no real growth in the economy last year. I can only suggest to the Minister of Finance that he may find that the government of Louis St. Laurent was doing something right, and what I suggest they were doing right was that they were following responsible fiscal and monetary policies.
I notice in the throne speech that the government seems to have discovered the marketplace. The government has found that there is such a thing is private initiative. The government has even become alarmed recently at its own level of spending. I welcome this "Johnny-come-lately" approach, though I notice that Canada's greatest problem, that of foreign trade, is virtually ignored in the throne speech, as it was in the speeches of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, we have been living beyond our means for some time, yet the government has done little to correct the problem. Canada's credit rating around the world has been jeopardized as international bankers have become alarmed at our increasing deficits, our rising foreign debt, our high inflation and lack of productivity in industry. We need, and in fact have needed, this credit, in international terms, to keep afloat. The present administration has been balancing its international accounts by adjusting our monetary system so that the provinces, municipalities and corporate concerns in this country have become big borrowers in international markets.
For example, last year it is estimated that Canadian borrowers took down one-quarter of the total amount borrowed internationally by all the countries in the world combined. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, a country with the resources we have in Canada having to beg and borrow all over the world to cover our huge trade deficit! In this connection, I think the House would be interested in a speech made only last week by Dr. Peter Campbell, vice-president and director of Wood Gundy Limited. He made a speech in Montreal pointing out the magnitude of our foreign borrowing in international markets. He also pointed out that this foreign borrowing was

encouraged by some of the moves made by the former minister of finance, John Turner, whom we all recall withdrew the withholding tax with respect to provincial borrowings and corporate borrowings offshore.
The fact is that if you review the figures put forth by Dr. Campbell, you discover that in the first nine months of this year the total amount of foreign borrowing by Canada was almost $7 billion. That is the amount that the corporate, municipal and provincial sectors have borrowed offshore or in the United States, which means that almost 50 per cent of the total debt incurred by those various sectors was actually borrowed from outside Canada. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first let me congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply on their very fine efforts. I am pleased to see the tone of optimism and confidence that marks the Speech from the Throne that has opened this second session of the thirtieth parliament. It reflects, in my view, more of the underlying reality of Canada and its future prospects-in spite of the problems it obviously continues to have-than the tone of pessimism about our future that marked the Prime Minister's interviews at the end of last December and his more recent speech to the Liberal party caucus conference in Toronto.
At the end of 1975 the Prime Minister spoke about the failings of the market system. Now the Speech from the Throne and the government's working paper places Canada's future primarly in the hands of the same market system. They commit the government, not to replace it but to make it work better, with pledges of due attention all the same to social costs and concerns. The Prime Minister's speech in Toronto a few weeks ago had in it a note of pessimism and doubt about the future of the Liberal party, as well as the more important issue of the very future of Canada.
However, none of this kind of concern and pessimism is at all evident in the Speech from the Throne, which is as much a statement for which the Prime Minister and his government take responsibility as any speech they may make directly in their own names. For example, the Speech from the Throne says that "Canada has better reasons for confidence and optimism than has virtually any other nation; that the fundamental reality that will guide our deliberations is that Canada is entering upon a decade of opportunity".
As Dickens wrote in "The Tale of Two Cities" about another turbulent period of history over 200 years ago, "It was

the best of times, it was the worst of times". Many would say the same thing about our own times. However, they are likely neither the best nor the worst. The reality is likely somewhere in between. Perhaps that is why the government in the throne speech opts for the middle road in its policy direction. If such a term is reassuring to many, at the same time it can raise questions as to exactly what it means in terms of government leadership and action.
If the tone of the throne speech is one of relative optimism, confidence and serenity, I think there could be more in the speech in the way of words of clear and passionate commitment by the government to the ideals and objectives it wants to achieve or wants to see Canadians strive toward. If there was a major threat to Canadian unity, one as great as any since the conscription crisis, as had been earlier suggested by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), one could have expected the speech to have more of a tone of absolute commitment to preserving Canada as a united country from sea to sea.
Speaking of commitment, I wish the throne speech had expressed as strong a commitment to greatly reducing unemployment as the one it expressed to continuing the fight against inflation. We have had some significant progress in the past 12 months in the fight against inflation, but we have seen little progress in the fight against unemployment which has remained stuck at the 7 per cent level for all too many months.
The throne speech speaks of the government's desire to create new, year-round direct employment programs. This is welcomed, but I seem to recall a similar announcement earlier this year when it had to answer those who said there would be harmful effects for hundreds of thousands of Canadians when the cutbacks of eligibility for unemployment insurance and other limitations it proposed in the last budget went into force, especially in the less developed regions of the country.
I hope the direct unemployment programs proposed in the throne speech will be soon set up and will be successful. However, unless the government departs from the objectives stated in the speech, of much less government intervention and a restriction on future growth of government, one cannot expect such direct employment programs to create enough jobs to make a real dent in current unemployment figures. These programs will be useful but they cannot be a substitute for satisfying jobs in the private sector, producing goods and services which add to our exports and generally add to our economic wealth and gross national product.
There must be more attention shown by the government to getting the economy moving than the government appears as yet ready to do from the words of the throne speech. The time has come for action to deal with our high interest rates, the high value of our Canadian dollar which makes our exports more expensive in world markets than those of our competitors, as well as action on certain specific kinds of tax cuts and measures to improve productivity.
The Speech from the Throne and the government's working paper point to the contribution the market system has made to our country's development until now and which it can make to its future development. Both documents explain why the gov-
October 21, 1976

ernment has decided to take what it describes as a middle road between greater government intervention and relying primarily on the private sector. However, these documents convey the message that it will in fact be relying more than ever on the market system and private enterprise as a means of allocating resources and of enabling Canadians to achieve their personal objectives of growth and well-being.
The throne speech talks about examining government programs to see which ones might be handled by the private sector. I believe all government activities and programs should be reviewed on a continuing basis to ensure they meet current needs and that their costs are in line with their benefits. However, we should not forget that the government has become involved in providing many kinds of services because of the unwillingness or inability of the private sector to provide them at all or to provide them at a cost and with a degree of access satisfactory to Canadians generally.
The government must make sure that it takes no decision to turn any of its current activities or programs over to private enterprise without making certain that the quality of the service and its availability to Canadians will not suffer. It is argued by some that the handling of activities by the private sector that are now carried on by government will enable better indentification and distribution of the economic costs. However, Mr. Speaker, there are social costs as well as economic costs involved here.
For example, market forces do not, and cannot, do a satisfactory job of ensuring product safety or preventing products from being sold that cause injury or death. Consumer protection legislation in the area of food and product safety has a cost, but there is also the often greater cost to the individual and his family and to the entire community arising from harm caused by unsafe products. There is also the matter of defining product quality.
Economic costs cannot be the only factor to be taken into account in assessing the impact and desirability of government regulations and programs. There are considerations of health, safety and social justice to be borne in mind. The benefits of the regulations and programs may well be found to outweigh their costs when all of these aspects are taken into account.
Over a year ago the government made promises similar to those made in the throne speech to the effect that there would be less government intervention and a review of government activities to see which ones could be reduced or turned over to the private sector, if not eliminated completely. These promises were a major component of what the government said was to be a comprehensive "attack on inflation", according to the white paper with which it launched the controls program. But since then on several occasions I have asked how that review promised in the white paper was to be carried out, by what department and also what minister would be in charge of this effort. There have been no answers or any indication that the work has even been started.
Before one can become too enthusiastic about the possible useful results of most recent proposals which are similar to those in the anti-inflation white paper of a year ago we should,
The Address-Mr. Gray
I think, have some answers as to how they are to be carried out, by whom and over what period.
There are a number of topics which quite properly are specifically mentioned in the Speech from the Throne; bilingualism, the fight against inflation, human rights legislation, and so on. However, one has to say that the speech is also notable for what is not specifically mentioned in it. There appears to be little directly stated in it for the Canadian consumer. In fact, I do not think the word "consumer" is to be found anywhere in the speech. It can be argued that the Canadian consumer will benefit from a successful fight against inflation, and that the second stage of the competition policy mentioned in the speech will have important though indirect benefits for the consumer, at least over a period of time.
As I have said, while there is direct specific reference to programs, for example for business and labour, there is no equivalent specific mention of programs for the consumer. The current throne speech does not mention a "comprehensive overhaul of consumer credit legislation" as did the October,
1974, speech, even though the press reported that late last year the then minister of consumer and corporate affairs was ready to introduce a bill to achieve this. That bill has not yet had first reading, even though the proposal for it was mentioned publicly before the 1974 election and was part of the election platform itself. The present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) has made reference to it in a recent speech outside the House.
It is, therefore, puzzling that the government as a whole, the cabinet, has not seen fit to make specific reference to this legislation in this throne speech. It is also puzzling that the speech makes no mention of a "total revision of bankruptcy law" and "improved safety of consumer electrical products", which were found in the speech of October, 1974. Both of these items were also part of the 1974 election platform.
The bankruptcy bill, with its important provisions giving new and higher priority for wages owed to workers in case of bankruptcy of their employers, at least received first reading in the last session and some study during that period by the Senate. This throne speech, however, gives no hint as to the government's intention about this bill for the current session. Also, improved safety of consumer electrical products did not surface publicly, at least anywhere during the last session.
The new throne speech does promise stage two of the new competition policy which would thereby complete the process of reform of our competition law which I began as minister before the 1974 election with the stage one bill, a bill that became law in January of this year. I think it should be of concern to consumers that nothing is said about the stage two bill finally making class action rights available for consumers and for small businessmen as well.
These rights are important to consumers who are harmed by uncompetitive or unscrupulous business activity contrary to our combines legislation. The right to sue through class or representative action should have been adopted as part of the
328

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. Gray
first stage legislation. This had been my own announced intention. The government should commit itself now to putting it into the second stage bill, along with a general trade practices jurisdiction. The latter step is needed to help stop the building up of conflicting and overlapping provincial trade practice legislation, which is coming to mean differing standards of protection against the same kinds of unscrupulous business practices for consumers, depending on where they live. Overlapping and conflicting provincial legislation also means harmful and unnecessary uncertainty for business as to the rules it must follow. In any event, the government should make a commitment to introduce the stage two legislation as soon as possible.
A major concern of both Canadian consumers and producers, food policy, is almost ignored in the throne speech. It is skipped over in a couple of brief and opaque sentences to this effect:
As a further element of the government's food policy, measures will be introduced to make more farm-stored crops eligible for advance payments. The government will also work with the provinces and farm organizations to strengthen the structure and productivity of Canadian agriculture.
There is nothing in the speech about developing a comprehensive food policy covering all elements of the food chain from producer to consumer. Yet there have been growing expressions of concern by Canadians generally about the seeming confusion and conflict in the government's present approach to food policy. There is the awareness of the world's need for food and the fact that Canada is one of the few countries with the potential and capability to be an exporter of food. There were hints before the throne speech from government spokesmen and, in fact, more than hints, that food policy was to be a major thrust by the government in the new session. It is, therefore, surprising and disappointing that so little is said about this in the throne speech we are debating now.
The speech conveys the impression that there already exists a government food policy which is comprehensible, comprehensive, and working well. That there is not yet this kind of policy is demonstrated if one looks only at the evidence provided earlier by the egg marketing situation and more recently by the industrial milk situation. Surely the time has come for the government to commit itself to a parliamentary review of its existing food policy. More important, surely the time has come for the government to work out and present proposals for a comprehensive national food policy covering all elements of the food system from producer to consumer. This is something that deserved specific reference as a government commitment as much as any of the other subjects mentioned in the throne speech.
The all too brief reference to food and agriculture raises as many questions as it answers. Increased productivity is a commendable objective, but in the light of the surpluses we have had, first in egg production and at least until recently in dairy production, the problem in our agriculture is certainly not one of surplus. Instead, it is one of how to find ways that meet the needs of the world and Canadians for an adequate supply of reasonably priced nutritious food.

Efforts to improve productivity in secondary manufacturing deserved mention in the speech no less than that given to productivity in agriculture. A specific statement of a thrust in this direction should have been in the throne speech in light of the justifiable concern both of the government and Canadians generally during the past year about declining productivity and, therefore, our competitiveness in world markets.
But to return to agricultural policy, surely the time has come to examine some of the basic assumptions of one of the key elements of the food policies we have, that is to say, the extention of supply management to more and more basic commodities. Many began, as I did, by being favourably impressed by the concept and supportive, as I continue to be, of what its proponents held out to be its basic objectives-fair income for producers and a steady supply for consumers at fair prices. But the government's efforts in supply management to date, especially in dairy products, have satisfied neither producers nor consumers. One must ask, after observing the developments over the past year or two in that industry, whether the supply of some of these kinds of products is capable of being managed at all, at least in the manner that has been pursued by the government.
At the very least, if there is to be a workable system of supply management, it requires a capacity for forecasting, foresight, planning and managerial competence that has not yet been demonstrated to a degree sufficient to justify having the government continue to base its efforts mainly on the present kind of programs. Also, a workable system of supply management must provide the consumer with the right to participate in it, not just in an isolated, minority way but as someone involved in the real decision-making of a process that affects the price the consumer has to pay for the commodity covered. This kind of consumer involvement has not yet been adequately established.
Developments in the industrial milk situation show that in recent months the government's program for it has brought increasing prices for consumers and reduced income for producers. Also, instead of even providing stable production it has created, first, an almost unmanageable surplus, and within less than a year the prospects of a shortage, of a lack of sufficient product, to meet consumer demand. The government's supply-management efforts have created instability of supply rather than the stability its proponents have promised. If the process of supply-management is to continue and to be extended, the government must demonstrate to Canadians generally the ability of the supply management concept to work fairly and efficiently in the interest of both consumers and producers.
Canadians as consumers and as workers also want to be reassured that the anti-inflation program is operating equally fairly and effectively on the price side as the wage side. No amount of talking about the decline in the consumer price index will help persuade the Canadian consumer and the Canadian worker that the anti-inflation program is both effective and fair unless the Anti-Inflation Board also begins giving publicity to its decisions on prices equal to the publicity it gives to its decisions on wages.
October 21, 1976

The board, by stating its decisions on the prices in the form of informal advice and guidance rather than formal rulings, has been able to say that the confidentiality provisions of the act prevent it from telling consumers what it has accomplished by way of specific price rollbacks. But in my view nothing in the act stops it from stating as a formal ruling, which is something the act does allow to be published, its agreement to the compliance plans it accepts from a company found to have excess revenue-rulings which set out the price rollbacks and the names of the products in question. The board apparently is now taking the position that the act does allow it to release the names of companies found to have excess revenue, but has not yet started doing this.
The same authority, in my view, also allows the release of the names of the products in question. Consumers have a right to know the names of the products involved so they can take advantage of the price rollbacks. This is particularly so if they paid too much for these or other products of that company in the first place, thereby enabling it to build up the excess revenue in question. Arguments that to disclose this information would harm the competitive position of companies are largely nonsense. If the information on price rollbacks is made public by the board at the same point in time that the company advises its customers of the price changes and thereby puts them in effect, that company will not be harmed competitively. And even if a competitor finds out beforehand about the price cut and reduces its own price to match it, well, so what? Surely the objective of the anti-inflation program is to encourage wider and wider general reductions in price levels.
In any event, the public interest and the need to confirm to the public the fairness and credibility of the anti-inflation program must be an overriding consideration. Also, since the compliance plans which the board works out with manufacturers and wholesalers do not cover the ultimate retailer of the product for which price cuts are agreed to, the retailer is not compelled to pass them on. Also, the program does not apply in a mandatory way to firms with less than 500 employees. So at present the only way to help make sure that the price reductions in question are passed on to the consumer is for the consumer to know about them and, therefore, be able to demand the reduction from their retailers; in other words, to set competitive pressures in motion to make up for the gaps I have mentioned in the application of the AIB's compliance plan.
The government says in the throne speech that it wants to encourage the market system to operate actively and to operate better. For this system to operate properly, information about products and their prices must be widely available to consumers. One way for the government to show its sincerity about what it says about its new reliance on the market system is for it to compel the Anti-Inflation Board, by amendments to the law if necessary, to disclose to consumers the names of products for which the Board orders rollbacks.
The Address-Mr. Gray

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Concern has, I think, justifiably been expressed about the approach of the administrator of the Anti-Inflation Act to his jurisdiction. An argument can be made that a worth-while amendment to the law is one which says the administrator cannot reduce rulings on wages appealed to him below the level set by the Anti-Inflation Board. However, whatever flaws there might be in the administrator's present jurisdiction, at least it provides a mechanism through which someone can review some of the rulings on wages made by the Anti-Inflation Board and can cut them back if he thinks they are too high. Where is a similar mechanism for prices? There is nothing available along the same lines for reviewing the board's decisions or private advice on prices.
I think there could be practical ways worked out for having a form of appeal from the board's decisions on prices, especially if all its advice to companies has to be cast in the form of rulings which can be published. There are ways of doing this, such as giving groups like the Consumers' Associations or the Canadian Labour Congress the capability to make appeals, or setting up an office of consumer ombudsman.
The recent Gallup polls indicate a paradox, such that along with a significant reduction in the cost of living there has been a growing lack of support for the anti-inflation program. It is true that the proportion of the total labour force that took part in the so-called day of protest was small-but a million Canadians were involved and that is still a lot of people. Most of the labour force may well have, quite correctly, decided to respect their contracts of employment and also that taking part in the protest was not the best way to get the government and parliament to change the anti-inflation law. However, this does not mean that they are all fully satisfied with the way they see the anti-inflation program being administered. Many of those who stayed at work may be ready to express their concern about it at the ballot-box at the first opportunity, unless in the meantime they are convinced that the program is operating fairly and evenhandedly on both wages and prices.
The government has not set out in the speech, or so far in the debate, exactly how it intends to carry out a process of consultation on new strategies for the post-controls society. However, it appears to me from the words of the speech that, unfortunately, while the government intends parliament to have a role in the process, it does not intend that role to be the central one. Surely parliament, and especially the House of Commons, must be the focal point of the consultation process on strategies and policies for the post-controls period, and I believe the best way for parliament to provide that focal point is through a special parliamentary committee on national goals. You will recall that I proposed such a committee in speeches, first in North Bay and later in this House last March. I suppose it is somewhat flattering that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has taken up this proposal.
However, I hope that his support for it has not weakened the government's ability to see its merits and to agree to put it into effect. Such a committee could provide a public forum for the presentation and discussion of points of view of both regional

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. Gray
groups and interest groups. It could be a forum of a kind not available in any other way. I hope the government will confirm its confidence in the parliamentary process by agreeing to the creation of such a committee in the near future.
This government, as is the case for every federal government, has an overriding obligation to strengthen and preserve national unity. This means efforts in the economic and social sphere. It also means confirming the ability of Canadians to deal with it in either of our two official languages. I believe in the importance and value of this policy. My belief in it was formed long before I entered the House of Commons and long before it was recognized and adopted by parliament as the official policy of the country. In my view, there is a quiet and moderate majority of Canadians which already believes-or at least which can be persuaded to agree-that the kind of Canada worth preserving is one that recognizes having both French and English as official languages as one of its greatest resources. It is a resource that helps give our country its distinctiveness. It helps our country effectively to present itself and its products to the world. It is important, as well in terms of simple justice so that Canadians, whatever their origin, can use one or the other of these two languages to communicate with their national government and their fellow Canadians.
But at the same time I think this quiet and moderate majority of Canadians expect the government to develop and apply measures to implement this policy which are both fair and reasonable and effective in terms of their costs. Therefore, to call for the application of the official languages policy in ways that are fair, reasonable and cost-effective is not the same thing as questioning the policy itself. I am glad the government has finally recognized this, as is evident from what is said on the subject in the throne speech. Steps along these lines referred to in the throne speech will, in my view, justifiably strengthen support for the federal official languages policy across this country.
I believe that there is much that is encouraging in the throne speech. While I have made some critical comments about it, they are intended to be of a constructive nature. I believe the speech, in general, is worthy of support.
To conclude, let me say that this is a time of concern for those who, like myself, want to see the government continue in office. In this connection, it may be of interest to recall part of what I said when I spoke in the debate on the throne speech which opened this parliament two years ago this month. I will not repeat those words here, but for those who, like myself, want to see the government operate in such a way that it will have the majority support of the Canadian people in the next election, the words I referred to may seem even more relevant today than they were two years ago.
We are at the mid-point of the government's mandate. It is, unfortunately, a point of decline in public support, judging by current Gallup polls and by-election results. To win back that support, the government has chosen what it calls the "middle road". The middle road for a Liberal government must not be just another term for small "c" conservative policies or a "do-nothing" policy. If there is a balancing effort between

private initiative and the market system-and community support for individual needs through government effort-it must result in action of a kind that has in the past meant electoral success for Liberals.
To achieve its objectives, the government must use the remaining time at its disposal to show itself to be a government that is truly compassionate and concerned-one that is people-oriented as well as being a government that is effective and efficient. It must be a government that is, in fact and not just in appearance, truly concerned with the individual Canadians and their needs, their hopes and aspirations for a better life. There is yet time, although it is growing shorter, for the government to convince the Canadian people, through its actions, that it deserves the kind of support the Canadian people gave it in 1974.
I, for one, am continuing my efforts, as must all those on this side of the House, to have the government operate in a way that justifies its receiving that kind of support. I believe that the government, on balance, continues to be better than its alternatives. However, the throne speech by itself is only a collection of words indicating potential, indicating intention. Therefore, I say that all of us on this side of the House must confirm our commitment to translating and developing those positive policies indicated in the throne speech itself, and those not mentioned but no less needed, into meaningful action in the interests of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I begin by expressing my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Harquail) and the seconder (Mr. Lachance) of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, and also congratulate the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) on his excellent speech. With facts and figures I believe he exploited the government's lack of credibility and its inconsistency in addressing itself to the real and serious problems facing this nation. I also appreciated the remarks of the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) who as usual made a vigorous contribution to this very important debate.
I think the remarks of the three previous speakers reflect the concern of most members of this House. Many of us have trouble in believing in the sincerity of this Speech from the Throne and the working paper which set the stage for the post-controls period. If we could place any confidence in the government to do all the things it proposed in the Speech from the Throne, we might have some hope that the nation could be led out of its current social and economic dilemma. In my view, however, this sudden about-face is yet another characteristic example of this government's erratic leadership since it took office in 1968.
The 12 innocuous bills which the government placed before this chamber today for consideration proves that it is either unable or unwilling to transform the platitudes expressed in the Speech from the Throne into reality. This government has waffled and wavered; it has been inconsistent; it has been devious; it has improvised, and it has been less than frank with the Canadian people. One year it leads with its left, and the next year it leads with its right. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has strained the good will and good nature of a vast number of Canadians. He has caused apprehension, concern and uncertainty by his pronouncements of last December, and now we are told the only hope for this country is reliance upon the free enterprise system. Just last December we were told it was not working; it was dead.
That sort of inconsistency is like a fairy tale, and that is unfortunate because running this country is a serious business. Are we really to believe that this government is genuine when it speaks of reasserting the role of the market system in a free enterprise economy, or is that merely a political gesture devised to overcome its current unpopularity? I hope Canadians will not again be hoodwinked and taken in by this ploy. Perhaps the results of last Monday's by-elections are an indication that Canadians will not be sloughed off with pious platitudes.
The Address-Mr. Mazankowski
In my view, Mr. Speaker, the government is not worthy of regaining the kind of support that the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) predicts. I believe it has lost the will, the capacity and the competence to govern. What was dished up to us in the Speech from the Throne and the post-controls document was an ingenuous and slick public relations pitch-perhaps more slick than we have ever witnessed in this country.
This effort to improve the image of the government has taken many forms. The Prime Minister and his cabinet have taken on a new profile of modesty and humility. We should pay attention to the jargon in the document and the way in which it has been distributed. The ministers have all stood in their places and given their respective sales pitches in an effort to merchandise this sudden turnabout.
Even the word "Liberal" is being downplayed during this debate. We have heard so much about the "middle of the road" that we are surprised they have not changed the name of the Liberal party to "the middle of the road party." This government has been swerving from shoulder to shoulder so long that it could be charged with being under the influence. The problem is, we do not know whose influence it is under, whether it is John Kenneth Galbraith, the DM-10, Keith Davey or the spirit of Mackenzie King.
The government has shelved its propensity for bigness and is committed to the philosophy that small is beautiful. It uses cliches such as "balanced growth", "quality of growth", "individual initiative" and is pledged to provide more government information. Mr. Speaker, this is the most secretive government in the history of this country, so it could hardly go any other way. Even the former minister of finance attested to that.
We have a hollow commitment to improve the lot of small business in this country, but most of us who have any experience in that field know that the actions of this government over the past eight years have done more to erode the confidence of small business than anything else. It has created a climate of uncertainty which has consistently affected the health and stability of small business, starting with the tax reform measures in 1971-72, overregulation, the way in which the Unemployment Insurance Commission has been functioning, the postal service, the impact of strikes and the competition from government programs. All these things have contributed to an unhealthy climate in the small business world, and we do not see anything in the Speech from the Throne to reverse the trend.
The public service has also been mobilized in this operation image, and this gives rise to the question of whether the government's motives are real and genuine, or illusory and deceptive. In that connection, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from an aricle by Stephen Duncan in the Financial Post of September 11. One section is entitled "Pulling out the stops", and it reads in part as follows:
Party stalwarts outside Ottawa are thrashing over fresh policy ideas. And, as two recent events in Ottawa suggest, the civil service is being recruited and mobilized to help the politicians.

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. Mazankowski
The first incident is a directive sent from Treasury Board Secretary Gordon Osbaldeston to the deputy ministers of each department, asking them to contribute to an "image ... of a cost-conscious public service." That is part of a government strategy (Osbaldeston's letter says) aimed at maximizing "the visibility and the public's awareness of restraint in government." Included was a request for lists of government programs that had been cut, and others that had been thought up, but never even submitted to Treasury Board for approval.
The second was a meeting of about 50 civil servants called together recently by the Privy Council office and the Prime Minister's office. They were told to itemize programs that had been initiated to improve service to the public. They were also asked to prepare lists of programs that were planned and could be announced immediately. And they were told to get working on new, innovative programs that could be announced in the near future.
Some good ideas and policies may emerge from all the activity. One of the problems plaguing the Liberals for the past two years has been the lack of a steady flow of really fresh ideas.
But the implication that policy planning now seems to consist of grabbing for new ideas almost at the last moment is unsettling. One well-placed civil servant terms the exercise "government by gesture".
His view (and it is a common one in Ottawa in the days leading up to the new session of parliament) is that the government, strung by unpopularity, will react with gesture rather than substance in the months ahead. The focus, that is, is on the image.
That summarizes the spirit in which documents were produced to this House this week. If the contents of this article are true, we must question the propriety of senior civil servants engaging in such partisan activities. Obviously if we are to be governed by gesture, by an administration concerned only with the short-term political interest, by a group concerned with grooming rather than governing, concerned with its image rather than with the real concerns of Canadians, there will be no joy for anyone.
I turn, briefly, to another area of concern to Canadians. I submit that Canadians have lost confidence in the financial control and management exercised by the Government of Canada with respect to its departments and agencies. I note with dismay that neither the Speech from the Throne nor the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) provide much hope for significant improvement in this area. One would think that considering the government's desire to be all things to all people, it would place high priority on this important area of our parliamentary democracy.
Surely the restoration of confidence in our system, the restoration of people's belief that taxpayers' money is being wisely and prudently administered, is at the core of the very foundation on which responsible government can continue to exist. It is true that we have seen a commitment regarding the introduction of a new Auditor General's Act, but before we become over-zealous about it we must see precisely what the objectives of the bill are and if the recommendations of the Wilson report will be followed. For example, will the legislation define the right to report on expenditures when value for money has not been obtained? Will it include the provision for the appointment of an accounting officer with respect to each appropriation? Who will be given responsibility for accounting in a proper manner, and for properly administering funds voted under an appropriation? At present not only do senior levels of the public service administer policy; they play an increasing role in the formulation of policy. In short, we want

to know how many of the 47 recommendations will be included in the legislation? How many other recommendations previously advanced will be incorporated in it?
People's concern over the mismanagement of the country's finances has not grown up over night. It has grown at a dramatic rate since 1968, at a rate commensurate with the government's deliberate actions to reduce the effectiveness of members of parliament, its propensity for secrecy, its distortion of the rules, and its attempt to downgrade the role and effectiveness of the Auditor General. It is little wonder thoughtful Canadians have become deeply concerned. They are especially concerned about the dramatic increase in government spending, particularly at the federal and provincial levels, spending which takes up over 42 per cent of the Gross National Product. In the United Kingdom that figure now approaches 60 per cent.
In the July issue of the Parliamentarian, Right Hon. Edward du Cann, chairman of the Select Committee on Public Accounts in the U.K., wrote-I quote from page 153:
It is not necessary, I hope, to argue the need for control. Government expenditure is, I believe, the largest single inflationary influence in the United Kingdom ...
I am in no doubt that firm control should be established, and by members of parliament in general...
Canadians are concerned that parliament has lost control over the handling of the nation's finances, that it cannot scrutinize as well as it should government expenditures, and that we are being governed by order in council. Above all, people are concerned because the state of the financial management, and control systems of government, its departments and agencies, is significantly below acceptable standards, quality and effectiveness. We obviously all have legitimate reason for concern, Mr. Speaker.
In a minute I shall quote from the proceedings of Public Accounts Committee, issue No. 52, dated March 30, 1976. Before doing so I wish to pay tribute to the outgoing chairman of the public accounts committee, and committee members, who have effectively examined government control and management systems in this country. Unfortunately the public and press have not given them the recognition they deserve. I think the House ought to commend them for the work they have done.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
I shall now quote the words of the Auditor General, Mr. J. J. Macdonell, as recorded at page 52:22 of the committee proceedings. He said in part:
I must apologize that some of this is fairly technical, but we feel very strongly about the fact that unless the systems are corrected the day may well come when I really cannot give a clear certificate on the accounts of Canada. I hope it does not come.
Mr. P. Lafferty, of the Auditor General's office, told the committee about lack of control. As recorded at page 52:18 he said in part:
... I would like to point out two concepts of control which are not being observed in the departments. The first is the segregation of duties and there is a

fundamental principle, that an auditing student learns within his first week, that you segregate duties down into the clerical level. The broad concept is that there should be careful segregation of duties so that, without unnecessary duplication of effort, one staff member, one element of a system, maintains an effective independent control upon the integrity and accuracy of another. It is this fundamental concept of one clerk, or one element of a system, balancing with another that does not exist in most of the cycles.
I list here the words: It does not exist in the expenditure cycle at two levels.
It does not exist at the clerical level, where there Js a lot of repetitive checking...
It also does not exist in the signing of documents. Cheque requisitions, in many departments, are signed by one official who has, virtually, an unlimited spending authority, to spend the money and approve his own requisitions and this directly contravenes Treasury Board policy.
At page 52:20 Mr. Lafferty is reported as having read the following words from the Auditor General's report:
These fundamental weaknesses result in incomplete or inaccurate financial information and in inadequate protection against fraud and error.
At page 52:11 Mr. Macdonell, the Auditor General, is reported to have said:
What worries me quite a bit is the fact that if there is fraud occurring there is really not much evidence of important ways by which it can be detected. To me, this is the major weakness.
As recorded at page 52:6, Mr. D. L. Meyers talked about financial controls and audit mechanisms. He said in part:
The chapters on financial control and internal audit deal with control problems within the accounting system. The problem here is not one of knowing what should be done, or agreeing to it. Indeed, the principles have been applied for many years in large organizations, both public and private, and are enunciated in the Treasury Board Guide on Financial Administration. It is more a question of failing to recognize the significance and the need for adequate internal control, and giving it the priority required at the department level.
An example of this is the photocopy of a cheque which I have attached to these notes. Please note that this cheque is blank as to the amount and the payee, but has already been signed-in this case, to improve operating efficiency. The rule here is simple, and to the best of my knowledge not disputed: blank cheques should not be signed. Yet I was personally able to obtain this example after my first day of reviewing controls in a cheque-issue branch responsible for the preparation of 2,000,000 cheques per month.
He goes on to say:
Departments clearly break the fundamentals of internal control: in segregation of duties, accounting control, effective supervision, and internal audit. In the context of a lack of effective budgetary control and management reporting, this not only leaves a strong possibility of error but also invites fraud, with little possibility that either would be uncovered.
What more glaring examples of waste, incompetence, and weak financial management could we have illustrated? There are many examples of non-compliance with the Financial Administration Act. Anyone who reads the report of the public accounts committee will find examples of waste, weak financial administration, and failure to comply with Section 26 of the Financial Administration Act. For example, and I quote:
For the Fiscal year 1974-75 nearly $1 million was spent by the Government of Canada for unused Crown-owned or leased accommodation. At the end of the same year approximately $3.8 million was expended on a new pay system which had to be suspended because it was deemed unworkable.
It later states:
Your committee, however, was most concerned with the action taken by the National Energy Board during the 1974-75 Fiscal year. The funds appropriated
The Address-Mr. Mazankowski for its operations by Vote 50 had been exhausted before the fiscal year end, and instead of attempting to obtain additional funds through supplementary estimates, the National Energy Board arranged to have $90,000 of its operating costs charged to the operations of the Energy Supplies Allocation Board. Furthermore, no subsequent attempt was made by the officials of either Board to correct this arrangement.
Having received evidence from all parties concerned, your committee has concluded that the action taken by the National Energy Board clearly contravened Section 19 and subsections (1) and (3)(a) of Section 26 of the Financial Administration Act and was illegal. Your committee strongly disapproves of the arrangement of funds made by this Board and recommends that disciplinary action be taken immediately by the minister.
As I said, this did not happen overnight. The government has whittled and chipped away at the parliamentary system. It has scuttled the effectiveness of the Auditor General. It has impaired the ability of parliamentarians to scrutinize effectively, analyse, and challenge government expenditures based on a philosophy of easy come, easy go simply pass the mistakes on to the taxpayer. However, I and many other taxpayers are getting fed up with the government's incompetence and maladministration.
I want to turn briefly to an area of the Speech from the Throne which I find rather fuzzy. It has to do with the review of our government's spending programs and the possible transfer from the public sector to the private sector. The review procedure is not clear. The criterion is not established. We in this party feel that this is yet another opportunity to engage the services of more consultants as a result of the review, and probably more consultants following the recommendations stemming from this review.
We would like to see an independent review agency which would appraise and evaluate government programs on a continuing basis as to their efficiency and effectiveness. The agency should be independent. It should have the power to initiate an evaluation on its own. The results, and indeed the recommendations, would be made public. Such an agency would have the authority and expertise to examine fully the effectiveness of ongoing government programs, their efficiency, and indeed have the power to recommend changes in the structure of any major government undertaking. Such a mechanism is certainly not unrealistic given the fact we are now spending well in excess of $40 billion annually. It could serve as an effective check.
This party would also like to see a review of our existing Crown corporations, some 60 in number. This party is committed to that. I am surprised that the government, with its new middle-of-the-road philosophy, did not propose that. Some studies on this have been done by important people. Doctor Alan Blair, an associate professor at Carleton University, engaged in a study and evaluation of 11 Crown corporations. During the course of his evaluation he found conclusive evidence that over half of them could be disbanded without any detriment or loss to the public interest.
We feel there is room for an evaluation of our 60 Crown corporations. Some were established with a specific purpose in mind many years ago. That specific purpose has now passed. In the interim, there must be more effective measures to scrutinize the operations and control of Crown corporations.

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. Stollery
Crown corporations are not accountable to parliament in the way they should be. For example, Air Canada has not been before a committee of this House since 1973. Surely with a major Crown corporation of that size it should be mandatory that it appear before an appropriate standing committee of parliament once a year to review its operations and annual report. This government does not believe in the function and real role of parliament.
In conclusion, parliamentary authority and control must be restored if the institution of parliament, and indeed politicians are to regain the confidence of the Canadian people. Now is the time when parliament should be strong. Canadians suffer from failing hopes. They are deeply concerned about the future and generally have a lack of confidence in those who are in charge of Canada's destiny.
We have many problems, social and economic. We have problems of national unity. There is cynicism, there is mistrust, there is apprehension, and there is irritation in this country. One basic and fundamental way of meeting these serious challenges is to restore and reinstate the supremacy of parliament.
I sincerely regret that the initiatives proposed in the Speech from the Throne are less than satisfactory. They are initiatives of gesture rather than substance.

Mr. Speaker, I First want to congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply. Having performed that task, I know how difficult it can be. I also want to congratulate the new ministers and wish them well in their portfolios.
The Speech from the Throne provides an excellent opportunity for members to speak on subjects that are of concern to them and their constituents. This tradition is one of the best in the House of Commons. Any of us can get up during these few days and get things on the record that we would like to have put on the record.
I should like to take my few minutes to direct attention to the indication in the Speech from the Throne that there will be amendments to the Immigration Act during the present session of parliament. The new minister-and I wish him well in that difficult portfolio-indicated the other day that we could expect a new act during this session.
Generous immigration policies have been good for Canada. But for the last several years in reaction to what was possibly-and I use that word with a question mark-an overly-generous system between 1969 and 1972 we have over-reacted and made immigration too tough and too difficult. I believe we are doing this to our detriment and to our loss. I want to take this opportunity to make that opinion very clear.
I was a member, and a pretty regular member, of the special joint committee on immigration policy which produced the report with the orange cover. It was an exhaustive study. We

heard hundreds of witnesses, I guess, and the committee produced 178 paragraphs of recommendations about what the government might incorporate in its new immigration policy, which presumably will be presented to parliament in the coming session. It was a good report. Who can argue when members of the committee suggest we should reform the provisions governing the prohibited classes? Who can argue against many of the reforms suggested by the committee in a variety of ways? As I look through the headings I see "Mental Retardation", "Mental Illness", "Epilepsy", "Contagious Diseases" and "Moral Turpitude."
Of course we have to reform those parts of our immigration policy which are obviously outdated and out of touch with reality in 1976. But in our approach to this question there have been errors. We have fallen for the statistical approach. I recall that during all this debate we have been talking about population and population growth. I, personally, do not believe in scientific government. I never did. Scientific government did not build this country-bloodless, scientific government administered by bureaucrats.
