We completely abdicate in this approach to human issues the tradition and history that built this country. It is not often a member has the opportunity to quote himself, but I was looking recently through the debate on Bill C-58. I spoke in that debate. I was describing the Canada that I know, and I said at that time:
Surely in the House of Commons of Canada I should not have to emphasize our unique Canadian experience-two founding peoples pioneering a country on the very edge of the habitable world, in spite of snow and ice and everything possible against us, and succeeding in establishing Canada. Canada is a remarkable country because it should not ever have existed.
We exist in spite of the trials our forefathers went through when they came to this country, and they did not do it by scientific government. Yet people tell us, "This group will go here, another group will go there, and this is what the population will be," and so on. I find this whole approach which we seem to be following in the area of immigration, baffling.
Goodness, will any member of that committee forget the charts with which we were presented illustrating the dire consequences ahead of us in the year 2,000, the predictions as to what the birth rate might be? I recall similar predictions 20 years ago concerning the province of Quebec. I remember it being said in Toronto that Quebec was a francophone province, that New Brunswick was a francophone province and that, bearing in mind the birth rate in Quebec, it would not be long before there would be a third. Today we all know that Quebec has the lowest birth rate in Canada, something which presents a big problem both for Quebec and for the rest of Canada.
All this was conveniently forgotten when officials of the department presented us with all those statistics in favour of having a new act and restricting immigration. They implied that if we did not have this new act we would have no control over policy. Meanwhile those of us who follow immigration
October 21, 1976

matters find that the departmental officials have managed to cut immigration under the existing act by some 25 per cent by using regulations which never come before the House of Commons-I do not know whether they even go before cabinet.
I was looking through some of the quarterly statistics a while ago. One set of figures which immediately struck me referred to immigration from Portugal-4,370 immigrants were admitted in the first quarter of 1974. Remember, this was the year when they said we would drown with immigrants if we did not do something. Well, we did not do very much in the House of Commons but they managed to do something in the immigration department because the number admitted in the same quarter of 1976 was 1,272. All in all, immigration from Europe was cut from 20,205 to 12,616, practically in half, through the use of regulations which none of us ever got to see or which, at best, we saw only after they had been approved.
This is an important subject because this country is finding itself today in a crisis. We all know there is a crisis over bilingualism. We all know, if we are honest, and I know members opposite know the same thing, that there are many people in this country who are asking themselves if it is worth while making this country work, and if those people are successful we need not bother having a House of Commons because we won't be coming here. And we were elected to make this country work.
I think that areas like immigration are part and parcel of a seige mentality that has overcome Canadians. Some Canadians are saying that the barriers should be raised, and in raising the barriers we must remember that in areas like immigration we are dealing, after all, with an interchange of people and ideas. The same barriers must also go up in the area of bilingualism. We must remember the two things are part and parcel of the same issue.
A bilingual Canada cannot exist in a vaccum; immigration policy must be an essential part. If we start to restrict immigration, to say that for various scientific reasons we are restricting entry, we will have to take the consequences. Let me tell this House that at no time in my life have I seen our chickens coming home to roost the way they have been coming home during the last few months. Never before do I remember responsible Canadians asking themselves whether Canada is going to survive. I think that is a pretty fundamental question for this House of Commons, and if we do not face the issue we are making a very serious mistake.
Just to emphasize to what point we have come in this country, the kind of person who came here in a spirit of adventure and initiative, who came to find opportunities in Canada, cannot come any more. No longer can a young man or woman of 21 years of age set off for Canada, not knowing exactly what they want to do or what the future may hold for them. They can no longer work in Canada or work their way across the country. That is a thing of the past.
The Address-Mr. Stollery
I was born in this country, Mr. Speaker, but I am sure many of us have spent a lot of our youth travelling around the country. This cannot be done any more because there is no work. Immigrants have no status, they cannot get a work permit. We have effectively put a stop to the enterprise of people; we have told them that they cannot come to Canada any more and I think this is a very serious mistake.
If the government is proposing to present a new immigration act, let me say at this point that I am not certain that we need a new act since we can cut immigration back 25 per cent under existing regulations. I see my time is running out, Mr. Speaker, but as a member of this House who has great admiration for his colleagues on all sides, may I say that under the present policy I would not be able to come to Canada myself. I feel that there is something fundamentally wrong.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to commence my fairly short remarks with a compliment to those who moved and seconded the Address in Reply to this latest Speech from the Throne on the way they discharged their responsibility.
I have been reading various Speeches from the Throne since I came to this Chamber and I must say that this latest one struck a different note. I noticed, or seemed to notice as I reflected upon it, a strange lack of enthusiasm for this Speech from the Throne in its reception. This was noticeable in the galleries and it was noticeable among the public generally. I would say that the country at large has demonstrated about as much enthusiasm for this latest Speech from the Throne as the turkey does for Thanksgiving. I think there is a reason for this, Mr. Speaker.
As a comparatively junior member I have been struck by the fact that there is something that distinguishes this latest Speech from the Throne from most of the others, and it is that very little concrete mention is made of what the government plans to do. I was interested to see the list of bills which the House leader presented. I know that other speakers have made reference to this as well, but I cannot help but mention that the first bill in the list of bills to be dealt with was that tremendously vital and important item, the Historic Sites and Monuments Act.
I think the government must have in mind erecting a couple of monuments on a particularly memorable site, perhaps the site where the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stood when he told us that he had wrestled inflation to the ground. That year the Prime Minister did about as well in the battle against inflation as General Custer did at the battle of Little Big Horn-in fact perhaps not as well. Or perhaps the government is going to erect a monument at the place where the Prime Minister stood when he came back from his meeting with President Nixon and said he had made a tremendous breakthrough with the United States. Judging from the state of current U.S.-Canadian relations I think he was rather optimistic in describing it as a tremendous breakthrough at that time.
I should like to confine my remarks fairly specifically to the subject of freedom of information and to urge the government to consider seriously some initiatives in this regard. Before getting to the main matters I want to talk about in this respect, let me say that as a member of parliament from Atlantic Canada I find that there is a strange lack of priority given to DREE, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, Which is very disturbing particularly in view of the critical situation that has developed in Atlantic Canada as a result of the government's failure to provide proper economic leadership and a national energy policy. This situation has exacerbated the economic difficulties which DREE was originally conceived to combat.
Of course I am bound to say in all honesty that under this government in recent years the whole country has become economically disadvantaged, and perhaps it is not fair for us to expect too much in the Atlantic area. Nevertheless the fact remains, as those of us who come from Atlantic Canada know,

that we are facing a terribly delicate situation. We need assistance from the federal government on a temporary basis, as well as some long-term guidance, so that we can begin to create a national power grid or some kind of power pool involving some of the provinces adjacent to us which have greater power resources. This could have been done a long time ago.
We would also have expected and would have liked to have seen some indication in this Speech from the Throne that the government recognizes the need to give special priority to the Department of Fisheries, give it as it used to have, status in its own right. Instead, where we once had a separate department for fishing and, one for forestry, we now have no forestry department at all, although this is one of Canada's most important resources, and we still have the Department of Fisheries effectively merged or submerged in the greater Department of the Environment.
We also note in Atlantic Canada, where unemployment is very high, that the government is considering re-uniting the Departments of Manpower and Unemployment Insurance-I gather in the same arrangement that existed in past years when we had the National Employment Service. I think on balance that is probably a constructive thing to do, but one has to reflect upon the many millions of dollars in administrative costs, and the wasted effort that has been the end product of this very poorly conceived experiment of starting a separate entity called Manpower divorced from the UIC. It did not work, and probably will not work unless there are further modifications made, because employers for the most part do not use the services of Manpower because, for various reasons, it has not been effectively co-ordinating the resources and needs of the private sector and the services it was designed to provide.
There is another matter which concerns me very much which I should like to mention before I move into the freedom of information part of my speech, and that is the sorry state of transportation. I have quoted the following before in the House and I think it bears quoting again. I will go back to 1972 at page 808 of Hansard for the date of March 14 when the then minister, now the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), said at that time that he agreed with those of us on this side of the House who said:
-that a reorganized structure is necessary in order that members and the country generally can obtain more information, and obtain it more easily, about all aspects of transportation. With this objective in mind, I propose to bring before the House in the next session three important pieces of legislation on which work is proceeding at the present time. The first of those is a bill designed to reconstitute Air Canada as a separate Crown corporation, thus divorcing it, as it were, from the CNR. 1 will also introduce a Canadian National Railways revision act and a companion piece of legislation covering amendments to the Railway Act. Hon. members will know how involved and far reaching these changes are; they have been asking for them for the last two or three years.
That takes us back to at least 1970. The minister went on to
say:
These changes have entailed a great deal of work, which is still proceeding. I believe, however, that these bills are essential and I will bring them forward as soon as they are ready.
October 21, 1976

That is a good many years ago and we can only presume that, in the interim, despite the very excellent Estey report of last year which dealt with this very subject of divorcing Air Canada from the CNR or well as other things not much progress has been made by this self-proclaimed dynamic government since 1972 on what would appear to be a fairly straightforward, non-partisan piece of legislation.
That is not the worst of it. The present Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) appeared before the Committee on Transport and Communications, and he promised on April 6 of this year a new national transportation act, a new ports policy, and a re-examination of the St. Lawrence Seaway.
Then we have to remember that, a year previously, his predecessor announced that a regional third air policy would be coming soon. The only reference to transportation in this present throne speech mentions that there are to be changes introduced to the National Transportation Act to protect against unfair freight rates.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What's wrong with that?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There is nothing wrong with it, I want to say to my friend opposite, but it is too bad the government would not give us a little bit of action and less verbiage. They are all swank and no knickers.
Let me now move to the topic of freedom of information. In our highly developed and technical society information, or rather its possession, has become a tremendous source of power, if not the prime one. At the turn of the century Max Weber asserted that the source of bureaucratic power was the "knowledge of files". That is even truer today than it was in his time. Modern governments are really hugh information processing machines. As the importance of information grows so does the need to make it available to the public.
If opposition members of parliament, indeed all members of this House, are to criticize constructively and realize what is going on in this most important of all institutions, and if journalists are to report accurately the facts, and if ordinary citizens are going to make effective use of their right to express themselves freely, then it is absolutely essential that they be given free access to all government information, with the exception of matters involving national security and individuals' personal records.
The parliament of this country should immediately consider and pass legislation that embodies the following principles: government information is gathered and compiled utilizing public funds, therefore it belongs to the public; the government must prove that it is not in the public interest to divulge certain types of information to the public rather than the public having to prove that they have the right to the information; up-to-date indexes of all the various government reports and studies should be readily available in public libraries and in federal buildings, to a much greater extent than is now the case; the government should be required to provide the requested information within a stipulated period of time; and a person or group who is denied information should have the right to apply to an impartial tribunal.
The Address-Mr. MacKay
I want to mention a couple of incidents, perhaps three, that I think should be brought forward in the context of these remarks. Kenzie MacKinnon, a Nova Scotian law student, spent the summer working with Ralph Nader's consumer affairs centre studying the working of the U.S. freedom of information act. Apparently a CBC television program requested access to government inspection reports on Canadian meat plants. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) felt that this report was too technical in nature, and he went on to say it was such and would be prone to misinterpretation by parties not familiar with individual plants or the nature of the procedure carried out. He said this could result in a firm being subjected to unjustified commercial pressures in the public arena.
Since all Canadian meat plants that export to the United States must be cleared by U.S. inspectors, Mr. MacKinnon applied to the United States Department of Agriculture for the information. Under the U.S. freedom of information act he got the information for no charge, after a ten days' maximum waiting period. Mr. MacKinnon quotes the report as making the following statements:
The trolleys and chain suspending apparatus for beef carcasses were not being cleaned, and exhibited rust and grease.
Then he says the tunnel through which beef and pig carcases were being moved "was not maintained in a sanitary manner". Later he states:
Fixed objects of wood that were improperly cleaned were contacting product surfaces. Overheads were deteriorating and some overhead structures exhibited evidence of rust, corrosion and excessive grease.
If we had a proper freedom of information law in Canada perhaps the Minister of Agriculture might have been encouraged to improve the sanitary conditions of our meat plants instead of acting as a public relations man for the meat packing industry.
I want to deal next with the Walter Rudnicki case. In September, 1973, as this House knows, the then Minister of Urban Affairs, and the president at that time of CMHC, Mr. Teron, and other CMHC officials, met native leaders to hear a brief on the needs for a Metis housing policy. Mr. Rudnicki set up an ad hoc group to prepare policy proposals. Mr. Rudnicki distributed policy papers at meetings with officials of the native council in order to get some feedback and because the minister and Mr. Teron had agreed to keep in close and continuous consultation with them. Apparently when the minister found out that policy proposals had been shown to the native people before he had seen them he hit the roof. He told Mr. Teron that either he had to go or Mr. Rudnicki had to go. Mr. Rudnicki was dismissed for violating his oath of secrecy regarding Cabinet documents. Mr. Rudnicki's secretary was also hounded out of the civil service.
Mr. Rudnicki sued in court for wrongful dismissal. He won his case and won $18,000 in compensation. The judge did not accept Mr. Teron's version of the events, which is a pretty polite way of saying he considered him less than honest. Judge O'Driscoll, who heard the case, referred to Mr. Teron's definition of what constituted a Cabinet document as "absolutely

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. MacKay
astounding". There were indications that the disclosure of documents was used as a pretext to get rid of Mr. Rudnicki who was too innovative an activist for the CMHC.
There is a third case that concerns me, and this is something I have referred to before in this House. It involves a couple of RCMP staff sergeants who, in my opinion, were dealt with in a very, very unfair manner.

speechtext: Shoddy.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, shoddy is a good word. There has been much opportunity for the government either to have justified their dismissal or to have made some sort of reparations to them. They were hardly run of the mill officers. They were both outstanding police officers, Mr. Don McCleary and Mr. Giles Brunet. I have had the opportunity to look at many documents involved in this case. One thing I found most outrageous was the memorandum from the officer in charge of the legal branch, Inspector D. K. Wilson. It deals with the subject of Sergeant Giles Brunet.
First may I set the stage by saying that when these men tried to protect themselves against what they considered a lack of natural justice, and when they attempted to get any kind of a hearing and were unsuccessful, they had a counsel, Mr. Arthur Campeau of the Ogilvy Cope firm in Montreal, I believe a very outstanding lawyer, contact the Solicitor General. Correspondence was exchanged, and so on.
Then we come to something I find very incredible. I refer to the memorandum from the man about whom I spoke previously, Inspector D. K. Wilson. I am very concerned about the tone and the Alice-in-Wonderland quality of it.
One line of this memorandum on page 7, which is dated December 3, 1973, states:
It is not surprising either that there is at least the allegation, if not the fact, of influence peddling between the lawyer and the Solicitor General.
That, to me, is an incredible thing to have been said by a responsible man high up in the RCMP. If any member wants to see the entire memorandum I will be glad to make it available to him. It is difficult to believe that a man that high up in the RCMP would accuse his minister of influence peddling because this minister was courteous and understanding enough to listen to representations from a very eminent legal counsel who intervened on behalf of these two fine RCMP officers. That, to me, is an indication of a very sick attitude. I want to bring it out again at this time in the House of Commons.
I suggest it is obvious to just about everyone in the country that a freedom of information law is needed. It goes almost without saying. It is as true today as when the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) first brought it up. Incidentally, the hon. member for Peace River told me that he had discussed this very subject with the members of the current Russian delegation visiting Canada, and he was told that the situation is about the same there as it is here.

The government is taking only baby steps toward this objective. Members of the government are dragging it out as much as they can. The throne speech tells us that the government intends to present a policy paper to the standing committee. The issue has been discussed, re-discussed, and discussed again. Now is the time for good legislation. I am very surprised that the present government has not jumped on this idea. This is not a party that is known to nurture along an idea, to fight battles for it. They leave this to the opposition parties. But the Liberal Party has the great ability to grab upon an idea when the time has come, and claim it for its own. There is no doubt about that. In fact after listening to the well paid public relations men of the government, it seems that members of the government are able to convince themselves that they originated the idea, fought the battles, and led the troops to victory themselves.
With the exception of the former finance minister, John Turner, who unknown to us all, until he left, had fire in the belly over this issue for years, the Liberals have not responded in their usual manner. They have not jumped upon the issue. Does this mean they have lost their touch, one more example of the downhill slide? This may be partially true, but I suggest there may be other reasons.
It has been proven that secrecy is fundamental to this government, that it is an essential part of its nature, perhaps even its true nature. This does not mean that the government is not willing to generate information. It is more than willing. In fact since 1972 the number of information officers has increased from 570 to over 1,000. The government in engaged in producing public relations pap, making reports two of three times longer than they should be, or glossing over a lack of substance with sheer weight of words.
It is not unrelated that, as a government becomes more secretive and hides more real information, it will turn out more false information, misinformation, or non-news. One reason I suggest the government ought to reassess its policy is that everything can be explained to the people on the single condition that you truly want them to understand. Lately the government has not shown that it really does want them to understand. One reason why the government will not be more open is that there is a feeling that the public is not competent to judge its behaviour. We have seen that indicated very clearly in the government's handling of the wage and price controls program.
The government has managed to alienate both business and labour. When these groups justifiably criticized the incompetency of the administration and the unfairness of the application of the regulations, did the government consider the possibility that there may be serious faults in the program? Of course not. The Prime Minister has told us that the Canadian public did not understand the program, and so he decided to spend a million or so of their tax dollars to innundate Canadians with snappy little ads telling them the error of their ways. That is his philosophy. If the government had any respect for the Canadian public it would quit wasting its money and come up with substantive changes in the program.
October 21, 1976

The other reason why the government will not move forward in respect of a freedom of information law of course, as has been demonstrated, is that there are things the government does not want to disclose. I want to point out at this time that the business of obscuring language is a mask beyond which stands out the much greater business of plunder. As time goes by we must watch very carefully that the special interest groups close to the government do not profit excessively by this relationship. That is another reason why we must have more freedom of information.
I suggest that, if all the facts were before this parliament, some of these gigantic projects that are making news, with allegations of hundreds of millions of dollars being spent unwisely at a time of restraint, might never have gotten off the ground in the first place, and we would all have benefited.
In one of his essays Montaigne relates the answer that a worthy Roman gentleman gave to the builders who offered for
3,000	crowns to alter his mansion so that his neighbours could not overlook him, as they then did. "I will give you 6,000", he said, "if you will make it possible to see into it from every side". It is as characteristic of this government to build a mansion into which no one can see, as it was of the above gentleman to has his conduct open to the public.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Cullen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in this my first address as the new Minister of Manpower and Immigration I want to pay a particular tribute to my predecessor, now President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras).

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Although I have had an all too brief acquaintance with this new department, I have come to realize the very heavy burden placed upon the minister in this department.
When one realizes that my predecessor held this portfolio for four years and that he did so in such a competent and capable fashion, one knows that this represents a significant contribution to the service of the people of Canada. I do not know how many of us can appreciate the countless hours of time and effort that had to go into the development of a new immigration policy and legislation, and I wonder if any of us can appreciate the tremendous amount of time required to consider the direction in which the department should go, the changes that should be made to the Unemployment Insurance Act, and the new employment strategies directed to helping unemployed Canadians. Couple this with the minister's responsibilities as a member of parliament for a very busy and
The Address-Mr. Cullen
active riding, his regular duties as a member of the cabinet, and the day to day problems that are bound to arise when one is dealing with unemployment insurance and immigration, and one can appreciate the heavy workload that the minister carries. Partisanship aside, I think all members in the House appreciate the contribution made by my predecessor. He has handed me a very difficult act to follow.
It is appropriate for me in this debate to comment on the very high calibre of the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply. As one who was given this honour a few years ago, I know the sense of responsibility that one feels when called upon by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to move and second the Address in Reply. I may say that the calibre of the speeches is definitely on the rise.
The government's key priorities have been outlined in the throne speech. One priority is the new immigration legislation. This is the product of more than three years of intensive work by my department, a major consultative process, of an invaluable study by a special joint committee of parliament composed of members of the House of Commons and the Senate. The bill that I shall shortly present to parliament will spell out the fundamental objectives designed to shape a forward looking immigration policy for this country. It will eliminate the outdated provisions of nearly a quarter of a century, and establish a solid foundation for a policy geared to the needs of all parts of Canada and able to rise to contemporary challenges, both domestic and international.
Another key priority will be the amendments to the unemployment insurance legislation. These will merge the commission and the Department of Manpower and Immigration into the new commission and department of employment and immigration.
Amendments will also allow us to take a more positive approach to unemployment problems through resource allocation. As the House knows, these amendments will change the five phase benefit structure to a simpler three phase structure, will set the minimum entrance requirements at 12 weeks, and will permit experimentation with the use of unemployment insurance funds for programs of training, worksharing, and job creation.
The changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act will result in a government saving of about $110 million next fiscal year. I am only referring to the government's saving on this aspect, not that of the employee and employer. The purpose of the amendments is not to save money; it is to let us and the unemployed utilize some of the funds now required for income maintenance to held provide jobs, incomes, and training. We are convinced that the income that goes with the dignity of work is preferable to the income that arrives in the form of an unemployment insurance cheque.

Mr. Speaker, there is no other priority more important than helping Canadians find a job. Today, our remarks will concern a new employment strategy aimed at creating what the

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. Cullen
Canadian unemployed wish and require: the dignity and the personal satisfaction given by a real job as well as a higher income than unemployment insurance. Today, the main difficulty is to increase regularly the number of jobs in the private sector. But in the next four years, the number of jobs could not increase too rapidly in relation with the number of Canadians seeking employment. Furthermore, we know that at the beginning of the 1980's, when the flow of young people seeking employment will have decreased, we could be in a different situation, that is we could have a shortage of manpower rather than a lack of job opportunities.

We must therefore look toward a strategy that will help to fill the employment gap over the next several years. It must be a strategy compatible with the restraint of expenditures, moderation in the increase of the money supply, and the avoidance of massive inflation-stimulating deficits. It must not be a strategy of major monetary or fiscal stimulation, vast programs of public construction or public service expansion, or major tax cuts; these would be incompatible with our need to reduce inflationary forces and to remove wage and price controls. Our basic aim is to reduce unemployment progressively over the next five years, without generating yet other problems.
It is my purpose today, Mr. Speaker, to outline the essential elements of a strategy that meets those basic criteria. The strategy is based on two fundamental premises: first, that the vast majority of Canadians need and want work and that there is work to be done, and second, that although income maintenance is essential for Canadians who want to work and cannot find jobs, our present substantial expenditures on income maintenance can be made more productive.
Our currently high unemployment rate is due to several factors such as regional differences, the particular problems of young workers, lack of skills, weak markets; employment disadvantages, and seasonality. Some unemployment is due to behavioural factors, but the problem facing most people is a simple lack of jobs or the skills to fill the jobs that open up.
There is no single cause underlying our unemployment rate and there is no single solution. But selective solutions must be pulled together into a single strategy. Our employment strategy alone will not cure unemployment. What it will do is to help keep unemployment down, and allow us to reduce unemployment progressively over the next few years in a way consistent with the removal of wage and price controls.
There are three broad thrusts within the strategy itself. The first is a comprehensive job creation program squarely based on community priorities; the second consists of youth employment and employability measures, to ease the transition from school to work for the young people who make up half the unemployed; and the third is a group of selective presentive measures to reduce the loss of work and hasten a return to employment.
The strategic approach that we are taking relies on a variety of programs being effective. Individual programs in the strategy will necessarily be changeable and flexible from year to

year; the program mix appropriate for 1977 may not be the best mix for the circumstances of 1979 or 1980.
The essence of the strategy is to get public work done and public benefits produced by people whose energies and talents are temporarily surplus to private sector needs.
We all recognize that a permanent private sector job is what Canadians most want, and that we must help them find it. But we must also recognize that when private sector jobs do not exist in sufficient numbers we have an obligation, both to the unemployed themselves and to the Canadian community, to make sure that people can have work and the incomes that go with work. From the point of view of both society and the individual concerned, work is far better than just giving people a cheque. The cost of unemployment is not just a loss of so many dollars or so much output. Much of the cost comes in failed career hopes; lost opportunities and eroded skills; in family stress, and in growing dependency on the working members of the community.
In 1977-78, the first full year of our five-year employment strategy, we plan to invest in the neighbourhood of $350 million beyond our regular expenditures on manpower programs. Over that five-year period much of the incremental funding for the employment strategy will come from changes in the unemployment insurance legislation. In the first full year savings to the government from the legislative changes will be about $110 million, but future savings will be even greater. Because unemployment insurance savings will rise as unemployment declines, we are looking at costs and resources averaged over five years. It is generally expected that, if parliament approves the changes I shall propose to the Unemployment Insurance Act, reduced government contributions to the unemployment insurance account will offset the extra costs of this employment strategy.
I shall deal first with the comprehensive job creation program. Because unemployment is at an unacceptable level we are allocating, as I said, about $350 million in expenditures in 1977-78 on special employment measures. Of this amount the largest single element will be a $200 million "Canada Works" program that will generate jobs for some 61,000 participants.
The program will be year-round, lasting up to 12 months when warranted, with projects tailored to local unemployment conditions. Funds will be allocated primarily to high unemployment parts of the country. Projects will be reviewed and recommended by ministerial advisory boards in constituencies, groups whose membership will change from year to year. The projects themselves will be subject to federal and provincial determination of broad priority areas. In parts of the country where the local tax base is inadequate, provision will be made for financial assistance with the cost of materials.
Investment in the Canada Works program will be adjusted to changing circumstances from year to year but the program will always operate on the basis that its role is to provide employment only when the private sector cannot. Wages will be based on the provincial minimum wage so as not to disrupt the private labour market. They will not exceed locally prevailing rates for the skills involved. Project workers will be helped
October 21, 1976

and encouraged to return to permanent jobs in the private sector. Project and selection controls will ensure that people are not drawn into the labour market simply to participate in the program. We will generally require project sponsorship by an existing community organization or group to ensure that real needs are met and the project is competently managed. The private sector-both firms and organizations such as chambers of commerce-will be invited to participate actively by sponsoring non-profit projects of community benefit.
A small portion of the $200 million for the Canada Works program will be set aside for temporary local employment emergencies-a natural disaster or failure of the main economic support of a community. We have developed emergency techniques in the last two years and have learned to respond quickly to such local disasters as the fires in Springhill and Main a Dieu in Nova Scotia.
The year-round program will be accompanied by a new program designed to supply jobs for about 21,000 extra students next summer. This program, "Young Canada Works", will have many of the same basic features as the year-round program. Some $30 million will be allocated largely to high unemployment areas. Project applications will be reviewed by the ministerial advisory boards. Projects will be up to 14 weeks in duration and sponsored by community organizations, including the private sector. Wage levels generally will be kept down to the minimum provincial wage levels. The range of potential projects will be the same as for the year-round program, but will be oriented to the interests and aspirations of young Canadians. The emphasis will not be so much on "doing your own thing," as on doing something of solid community value-such as fire prevention programs or environmental improvement.
The third new job creation element will be a Summer Job Corps in which we will invest up to $10 million. The Summer Job Corps will provide employment opportunities for students in activities related to federal government priorities. Projects will be sponsored by federal departments and agencies. Students may work on such projects as cleaning up rivers. For the most part, the work will be out of doors. None of it will be within federal departments themselves. Students will work in a structured environment under trained leaders, in any one of a dozen priority areas.
We will also continue, as part of the job creation component of the employment strategy, the existing summer student employment and activities program at a cost of about $25 million. Those funds will provide for a variety of initiatives by federal departments to create employment for young people; for example, cadet corps, and student-run summer manpower centres.
The Young Canada Works program, the student summer programs, the Summer Job Corps, and the main Canada Works program will all provide additional worth-while employment opportunities for young people, allowing them to gain valuable experience, while at the same time helping them
The Address-Mr. Cullen
to meet financial demands. But these programs, in themselves, can only partly respond to the long-term problems of youth employment in Canada because many young Canadians lack work skills and experience rather than job opportunity.
I now come to youth employment and employability. The second main thrust of our employment strategy is directed as much to the employability of youth in the private sector as the first is directed toward creating employment. Young people today have employment problems of a kind unknown to us 20 years ago. The problem is only partly a lack of jobs; in large measure it is the vast gap which exists between the world of school and the world of work.
Increasingly we see the tragedy of the young person who emerges from school, diploma in hand, but who cannot get a job because he or she lacks something called "relevant work experience." Young people today acquire knowledge of immense value in our schools and post-secondary institutions. But too often, employers tell us, students are not accustomed to the day-to-day realities of work, and are not able to translate text book knowledge into practical accomplishments. They cannot be hired until they can do so, yet they cannot get relevant work experience without being hired.
One remedy is to expand and strengthen what we can do to provide counselling and job connections for secondary and post-secondary students. We are proceeding vigorously with the publication of a full range of career counselling materials called "Careers Canada" and "Careers Provinces" for use in our Manpower centres and in co-operating school systems. We are developing, for possible introduction next year, a computer-assisted counselling program called "Choices". And we will strengthen and expand the Manpower counselling and job finding centres we now have on post-secondary campuses across the country. Over the next three years, we intend adding up to 18 new centres to the existing 70.
Better counselling information and techniques and a greater availability of counselling services will help, but they will not provide experience, and therefore can only be part of the answer for our young people. Counselling provides direction; "co-operative education" provides experience.
With the co-operation of the provinces I plan to give greater impetus to this concept of co-operative education which could successfully bridge the gap between school and work but which has been developing far too slowly in Canada. "In term" means simply that the teaching institution arranges with local employers that work and study will alternate in some sensible way. We know of over 80 such arrangements current in Canada. The young Canadians who have participated in them have had far fewer problems in the labour market, are far more certain of where their career interests lie, and are often hired by the very firms for which they worked as part of their training.
I have communicated with provincial ministers and offered to join with them to encourage and promote the development of more co-operative education. It is not an expensive proposition. No wage subsidies are involved. Most of what cost there is goes into setting up such programs rather than maintaining

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. Cullen
them. We will offer to share with provinces the costs of starting co-operative education programs, not perennial subsidies for the programs' duration. I am convinced that, as these programs get established, the advantages to employers, students, and post-secondary institutions will be so great that no further financing will be required.
We are also interested in taking this concept a step further for youth with serious job placement problems. As soon as possible I plan to initiate a program which will help young Canadians gain a foothold in the job market. That program, called the Job Experience and Training program, will have a substantial winter component and a smaller summer portion. It will be based essentially on the very successful experience that we have had in the last two years with chambers of commerce and boards of trade on a pilot project basis.
Next summer chambers of commerce and boards of trade across the country will be asked to arrange for the placement of students identified by co-operating school authorities as drop-outs or potential drop-outs for whom serious employment problems are anticipated. They will be given exposure to a work environment and employment counselling that will facilitate their return to school or their entry to the labour market. The chambers will be given a modest grant, and participating employers will receive a small wage subsidy. In the winter young people who encounter severe and continuing difficulty in getting and keeping jobs and need work experience will be provided with nine weeks of partially subsidized employment in the private sector, preceded if necessary by a brief training period. The result, at a very modest cost per hard-to-place young person, will be the acquisition of experience without burdening any firm because the government will, if necessary, help to compensate for the young worker's low initial productivity.
Next year we expect to invest a total of $11 million on these particular measures to help young people find rewarding and productive employment in the private sector. I am convinced that measures to improve career counselling and career choice, and to help young people blend schooling and experience, are among the most productive we can mount. If the programs are as successful as I hope, I would like to see them take an increasingly large place in our over-all employment strategy.
Next may I speak about preventive measures. The third major element of our employment strategy is the development of new and the strengthening of established preventive measures. The federal government now is investing well over half a billion dollars in the training and retraining of Canadians to increase their employability and income. Most of this very productive training is carried out in provincial institutions. Our first step will be to increase our manpower training budget for next year, with an emphasis on the expansion of industrial training. For some years we have been increasing the proportion of our industrial training, because of its high productivity and relatively low cost. In the past five years our funding of industrial training has increased 500 per cent, from $10 million to over $51 million originally planned for next year. We

will increase that by $19 million to a total of $70 million in 1977-78.
These training opportunities will particularly benefit young workers, women returning to new careers in the labour force, native people, and the many Canadians who each year find that they must acquire a new occupation to earn their daily bread.
With the expansion of industrial training and the introduction of the job experience and training program, the government is responding to suggestions from a number of quarters. As suggested in the government's working paper, "The Way Ahead", this is an area in which industry can assume a role that might otherwise be left to a government institution. I hope that business will accept this responsibility willingly and that the results will warrant expansion of co-operative business-government partnerships in human resource programs.
No comprehensive employment strategy for Canada would be complete without the provision of a more adequate level of opportunities for the many Canadians who are, in one way or another, seriously disadvantaged in finding and keeping jobs. Although my department already has a number of programs that provide a good deal of assistance to people with severe employment disadvantages-the Outreach program, intensive counselling programs, the Local Employment Assistance Program, and our developing community employment strategy- we can and should do more for the Canadians who are hardest hit by unemployment regardless of the state of the economy.
Accordingly, we are carrying out a major review of existing programs for the handicapped, with a view to promoting various measures to facilitate their integration into the labour market. I do not expect this to result in the imposition of hiring quotas or other artificial devices in the private sector. I expect that, in co-operation with the Public Service Commission, measures for handicapped people may be developed to expand their opportunities in the public service, improve their access to services, and provide leadership in showing what can be accomplished. Later in this session of parliament I hope to announce some new measures we will undertake and to suggest ways in which the private sector can join in these developments.
Today I can announce that we will expand the Local Employment Assistance Program by more than 40 per cent through the addition of some $6 million to the budget for next year. Over the last three years this program has proven to be highly effective as a means both of providing employment to serious disadvantaged workers and enabling them to progress to future employment in the private sector.
There are some innovations such as work sharing and occupational training. Thus far I have been dealing with programs in the context of a strategy for the next five years. Now I would like to touch on several innovations we wish to introduce in the new unemployment insurance amendments. We hope these will greatly strengthen our unemployment insurance program and make it not only the essential protection for
October 21, 1976

unemployed workers, which it is now, but also a positive instrument in promoting a healthier and more productive labour market.
The first of these measures we call "work-sharing". We plan to introduce next fall, on an experimental basis, the concept of work-sharing during temporary economic downturns that has been so successful in a number of European countries. The idea is quite simple.
At present when markets slacken temporarily, firms cut back their production and their work force. The people who are made jobless claim unemployment insurance, search for other work, or take training to get into new occupations. Typically there are major losses involved in this process- people's work skills erode when they are idle, spirits are depressed, and they lose the habits and patterns of work that are so important to personal and family stability.
Work-sharing avoids that problem. For instance, instead of laying off 25 per cent of the workers, a company and its employees agree that the available work will be shared and all of them will work a 30-hour week instead of a 40-hour week. The government pays unemployment insurance benefits for a quarter of the week to all the workers, instead of paying for the full week to one quarter of the workers.
Despite the extensive European use of these work-sharing programs and their apparent benefits to individuals and companies, the system has not yet been tried in Canada and we want to make sure that it will work here. After experimentation and assessment next year, we may find voluntary and temporary work-sharing arrangements are measures we wish to develop widely for use in short-term, non-seasonal slowdowns.
The work-sharing experiments will be developed and carried on by a very small but highly effective service, the Manpower Consultative Service, which my department has operated for a decade, and which we shall expand for this purpose.
The Manpower Consultative Service brings together companies, workers, and unions to develop an action plan for overcoming a variety of employment problems. Such problems may range from an impending shutdown, resulting from difficulties occasioned by technological change; problems associated with high turnover and chronic absenteeism; to simple problems of anticipated shortages of skilled workers. Although too little known, the Manpower Consultative Service is one of the most effective preventive tools we have. It eliminates, before they arise, many employment problems that workers and companies would otherwise face.
Another new productive use of unemployment insurance lies in the field of occupational training. Our plan is to encourage unemployed people who lack job skills to use their idle time to take training and prepare for the new jobs that will develop. Naturally we shall not train people who already have marketable skills; we shall train only for skills that we believe will be in demand. Unemployment insurance will partly replace our regular training allowances and thereby free funds to provide for additional industrial and institutional training.
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
We also plan to experiment with direction job creation projects in which unemployed Canadians receiving unemployment insurance will be offered the chance to participate in community service projects. We would, of course, maintain job counselling and job search activities so that they could move to regular private sector jobs that became available. But in the meantime they could protect their job skills and enhance their feeling of participating in activities of community value.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), right off the bat I must accuse him of plagiarism. Obviously he has dug up some Conservative policies and platforms of the fifties. All of this was implemented years ago. Six of these schools were established for technical and vocational training. It is unfortunate that the program was not continued by the Liberals. However, I congratulate the minister this evening on reviving this very successful Conservative program. I am sure it will be very successful.
I am familiar with the technical school that was established in Manitoba by the Diefenbaker government. I checked figures there. It has trained many Canadians, young and old, to a profession. In this it has been very successful. The minister is to be congratulated for continuing this Conservative program, even though there was a ten year lapse.
Tonight I would like to take the opportunity to extend my congratulations and best wishes for good health to His Excellency the Governor General, and Madam Leger. Their presence and participation at the opening of this session of parliament served to re-affirm our continued support of the monarchy which makes Canada such a unique nation.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
At the outset I believe I would be remiss if I did not take a few moments to extend my belated birthday greetings to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and to assure him that we on this side of the House spared nothing to make sure he got a resounding birthday message from the people of Ottawa-Carleton and St. John's West. If the Prime Minister were to call a general election for his next birthday I am sure the voters of Canada would be even more generous in their greetings and present him with an early retirement.
I will never cease to be amazed at what the Prime Minister will do to divert public attention away from the real issues facing Canada. A year ago the Prime Minister announced on Thanksgiving Day that his government had a well prepared contingency plan to fight inflation. Now, a year later, as the economic health of Canada continues to deteriorate, the Liberal government has come up with another act of governmental showbiz to cloud the issues.
What I am specifically referring to is the decision of the Prime Minister to send his cabinet around the country selling bilingualism. This is a red herring that the Liberal government is using in its desperate attempt to make as many people as possible overlook the poor state of the economy.

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
At the present time there are approximately 750,000 Canadians unemployed. This gets us back to the minister's statement tonight. The government never acts when it sees trouble on the horizon. Instead of acting when there are
200,000	or 300,000 unemployed, it waits until there are 750,000. It has to be absolute, complete, total disaster before its members say maybe they had better do something. Then what they do is dig up an old Conservative program because they have no ideas of their own. They are completely bankrupt of any original ideas. At a time when approximately 750,000 Canadians are unemployed, surely one has to wonder whether their priorities are totally mixed up, or are they confused? Under the guise of promoting national unity the Liberals have angered and frustrated many Canadians. This folly must stop and the government should start concerning itself with the key national problem-our economy.
As a member who came here first in 1972 I have to admit that even after nearly four years I still have a difficult time determining when the Prime Minister and his government are telling the truth and when they are not. When the Prime Minister publicly admitted in Saint John, New Brunswick, that the Liberals had lied on the controls issue during the 1974 election I was not at all surprised. It served to reinforce the question: when are the Liberals telling the truth and when are they resorting to falsehoods? For example, in the Speech from the Throne the following passage appears:
... the government will continue to practice fiscal restraint. The control of inflation will remain the single most important condition for economic stability in Canada, even after price and income controls are removed. Determined restraint in fiscal and monetary policy is essential to the long-term control of inflation.
These are worthy goals, Mr. Speaker, but looking at the record I find myself wondering when the Liberal government began to practice fiscal restraint and to control inflation. This is but one example of the doubt it creates. To say there is a credibility gap would be an understatement.
It is deceitful on the part of the government to pretend that bilingualism is now the burning issue of the day when no serious attempt has been made to restore health to the economy. Anyone taking a close look at the government's economic record would be bound to agree that ministerial priorities are confusing, to say the least. The last significant legislation introduced by the Trudeau administration was the controls program last fall. For almost 12 months the country was without any economic accounting, and the budget which did come down in May took no initiative in the economic field. Instead it left responsibility for restraint to the provinces, and responsibility for growth stimulus to the United States. Yet the government still acts as though our economy is in fine shape. Who are the Canadian people to believe?
Prior to last May's budget there were four events which had serious impact upon the economy. First was the resignation of finance minister John Turner who will be proven to be the most irresponsible minister of finance in Canadian history because of the way he allowed government spending to run

rampant. There was the about-face of the Liberals on the controls issue, and, of course, the Prime Minister's speech on his new society. Last I should mention the way in which the controls program was, and still is, being handled. Each of these events damaged confidence in the economy at a time when inflation, industrial disputes, and a worsening balance of payments deficit were only further testing the system. When such reputable groups as the Economic Council of Canada, the C.D. Howe Institute, and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce all share the view that our economy is in a mess we can be sure they are not exaggerating. It is small wonder the government is using diversionary tactics to take people's minds off the economy.
Government spending presents a greater threat to the future of Canada than any other which faces us. With a projected federal spending deficit amounting to $6 billion I am of the opinion that the Prime Minister and his cabinet should be explaining to the Canadian people how they intend to solve present economic problems rather than gallivanting around the country spouting rhetoric on the Liberal-created issue of national unity. Wastefulness and bureaucratic incompetence only bring us closer and closer to bankruptcy.
The annual report of the Auditor General presented last December confirmed a deeply rooted belief held by many Canadians that the Liberal government is the biggest culprit in bringing about the growth of inflation. In his last report the Auditor General served up columns of shocking news, horrible stories of mismanagement, bumbling, over-spending-black comedy at the expense of the taxpayer. From all the reports of financial mismanagement it is evident that the Liberals have lost their grip on government spending. Policy objectives are not being reached. Millions are being wasted because of official sloppiness, poor communications, and abrogation of responsibility. These have all become the trademarks of the Liberal Party of Canada.
People cannot fail to be concerned about what the Auditor General has to say with regard to the government's financial habits. In the face of the combination of high inflation and high unemployment which has sent the economy staggering, the government can no longer ignore the cry for better financial control in Ottawa. In his report the Auditor General stated, and I quote:
The present state of financial management and control systems of departments and agencies of the Government of Canada is significantly below acceptable standards of quality and effectiveness.
Soon after that statement appeared in the Auditor General's Report, the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), in his capacity as Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee, put the following question to the Auditor General:
Since the Auditor General is so critical about the financial controls in government departments, how can you assure the House that the public accounts and financial statements of the government are accurate and reliable?
The Auditor General's response was:
We feel very strongly about the fact that unless the systems are corrected the day may well come when I cannot give a clear certificate on the accounts of Canada.
October 21, 1976

I contend, Mr. Speaker, that this gives us a clear indication of the financial fiasco the Liberal government has led us into. The financial implications are such that one must wonder aloud why the government is employing accounting procedures which it would not accept were they used by a business or by a private citizen. Revenue officials have little patience with an individual whose books are not clear and accurate, yet the government is using methods about which the Auditor General has serious reservations.
The Liberal government has become a spending machine without a control centre. For the record, I should like to call attention to a few examples in support of that statement. The Department of National Defence, at the time of a national housing crisis, lost $214,000 on unoccupied housing in Halifax where there was a severe housing shortage. The Department of Supply and Services wasted $3.8 million on a computerized government payroll system which proved unworkable and had to be abandoned. The federal government paid $4.5 million for offices it did not use. The federal government has developed a bizarre practice of making loans to itself and then counting the loans as assets.
Those, Mr. Speaker, constitute but a tiny sampling of the gross financial misdeeds of the Liberal government. This is why I have serious reservations about the section in the Speech from the Throne which states:
You will be asked to consider a bill designed to clarify the duties and responsibilities of the Auditor General of Canada and to provide him with better means of fulfilling his important function as a servant of parliament.
My reservations stem from the past performance of the Liberal government which has failed to act on the recommendations of the Auditor General to put its financial house in order. Again, this goes back to my comments that it is difficult to determine if the government is telling the truth or using deception. Judging from their past performance, however, one can only assume that the Liberals are being less than sincere.
We on this side of the House have for some time been in favour of strengthening the office of the Auditor General. Time and time again our calls for implementation of his recommendations have fallen upon the deaf ears of the government. To date, little if any action has been taken on the report of the independent review committee with regard to the office of the Auditor General. Yet we are now asked to take seriously the government's pledge to assist that office. I hope members opposite are sincere in their intentions, Mr. Speaker, motivated by the way in which government spending has gone out of control, that this is not just political window dressing in a further attempt to con the public into thinking the government is actually serious about fiscal restraint.
A Progressive Conservative government would be committed to the idea of being prepared to be completely accountable to parliament for all government spending. At the present time the control of supply by the elected representatives is not respected by the Liberal government. It has reached the point
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
where spending estimates are presented in a form that cannot be readily understood. The public accounts are insufficient enough to let the government get away with unlimited spending.
Let me point out that it was the Liberal government that in 1969 changed the rules under closure and put an end to the proper examination of federal government spending. Now liberals have trapped themselves. They do not even know what is going on today. They are under the complete control of the bureaucracy. Not only are parliament and the public unable to assess the value or purpose of much of the government's spending, but even the cabinet, treasury board, department heads and program managers are unable to judge the worth of what they are doing. It is no wonder that the Auditor General has publicly stated that parliament has lost effective control over government spending.
It was somewhat refreshing to hear the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) a former cabinet minister, say to this House last week, as reported at page 83 of Hansard:
Whether the government is able to proceed down this middle road will depend in some part on how this parliament can control government spending.
The point I am going to make is that we do not now control government spending-
Then the hon. member for Scarborough East went on to say:
In my view it is urgent that we find new means of controlling government spending-
It is so ridiculous, Mr. Speaker, under the present committee system to examine the estimates after all the money has been spent. I suggest this is one of the most irresponsible actions of the government. Reviewing spending estimates after the money has been spent is an absolute joke. As I was saying, it was refreshing to hear a former Liberal cabinet minister come to grips with the evils of increased government spending and take a positive stand by offering what in many respects sounded like Progressive Conservative proposals.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has proposed certain action to be taken if we form the government. For example, he has called for the strengthening of the committee system in parliament by giving the committees investigative powers so that public spending might be better scrutinized. The actual record of the Liberal government, compared to its performance, can only lead one to conclude that it is a government that cannot be trusted, Mr. Speaker. Only a change in government will alter the trend of financial mismanagement.
There are, of course, other areas where the government has created a breach of faith with Canadians because it has said one thing and done another. Freedom of information is a perfect example of the double standards of the Liberal government. My colleague, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), has done an excellent job of bringing this issue into

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
the public forum and has shown leadership in the effort to make government more open. This is indeed a healthy move at a time when there is growing cynicism with government. Even the former member for Ottawa-Carleton has been crusading for freedom of information.
It would seem to me that the emphasis on freedom of information in the throne speech is another example of the Liberal government's attempting to use an issue for the sake of political expediency. It is interesting to note that the government has hit an all-time high in the use of terms such as "top secret", "confidential", "restricted", and so on to cover even the most trivial government documents. Yet it now expects us to believe that it is suddenly going to be open.
On September 7 Gordon Robertson, secretary to the cabinet for federal-provincial relations, said this in the course of a speech:
Most of the articulate argument in favour of increased access to government documents comes from special interests-the media, members of parliament-
He says members of parliament are a special interest group. We are here to represent the people.
-the pressure groups, and the academics.
What I find amazing about that statement, Mr. Speaker, is that an employee of the federal cabinet is insinuating that members of parliament are a special interest group. As elected representatives of the people I am sure that my colleagues share my feeling that an employee of the Liberal government should have more respect for parliament than to insinuate that it is just another group that is after government documents. I wonder what the real attitude of the Liberal government is on freedom of information.
I should like to take a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, to touch on the subject of bilingualism. For too long the Liberal party has used bilingualism as a political device to claim that it was the be all and end all of national unity. All too often in the past the public has been led to believe that this nation could only be united under a Liberal government. I share the sentiments of my leader who, on October 13, said that the manner in which bilingualism has been implemented has caused some concern among Canadians.
I can understand this concern among Canadians. The two ministers who spoke today, the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts), and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), came to Winnipeg and said that western Canadians are shoving English down the throats of the citizens of Quebec. That is all they said; they did not qualify it. I say that is a lot of nonsense. I find very little support for Bill 22 under which Canadians are being denied the right to learn English in the province of Quebec. That could only happen under a Liberal government. As I was saying, the Leader of the Opposition said there was concern among many Canadians, both French speaking and English speaking, but that there is no reason to call them bigots or racists.
Many moderate and reasonable Canadians are growing apprehensive about bilingualism because they doubt the

motives of the Liberal government. As the Leader of the Opposition has said, a government without trust cannot govern, because trust in a federal and diverse country like Canada is elemental to national unity. This government no longer has that trust, Mr. Speaker. Many Canadians have become apprehensive about bilingualism because of such things as the Liberal attitude on Bill 22 in Quebec, the practice of having middle aged civil servants take costly and unnecessary language training, rather than develop long-range programs, use of a quota system at the expense of the merit system, a bilingual labelling and packaging act which is hurting many businesses, and finally, over-all implementation of bilingualism.
I can only concur with my colleague, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner), who said:
The principle of bilingualism is only valid when it means the same to Canadians as the principle of fairness. This government has somehow managed to divide the two principles in the minds of many Canadians. That is the single, greatest tragedy of the present government. That is the single, most gnawing doubt that attacks the very gut and fibre of our country. There the record of this government is a record of failure.
The Secretary of State and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration also stated in Winnipeg that they were not shoving French down the throats of Canadians. I attended one meeting where the Secretary of State made that statement and I pointed out to him that this is what was happening. The government is forcing French television channels into areas where they are not needed or not wanted, as was the case in northern Manitoba, British Columbia, and St. Thomas, Ontario.
Yesterday the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt) related how the CBC was cancelling out an FM radio station in his area in order to bring in a French channel, and his area is 98 per cent English speaking. If I were a government member I would not be trying to shove an English channel down the throats of the citizens of Rimouski if they did not want it. I am sure Rimouski is about 98 per cent French speaking and the people there want French radio stations and French television stations. I say that the Liberal government is shoving French down people's throats in implementing the bilingualism program.
Some of the members of this party have attended CRTC hearings to oppose the introduction of these channels in areas where they are unnecessary. I hear a lot of rumbling on the other side, Mr. Speaker. Let them get up on their feet and say something about this. I am complaining about the implementation of the program on the part of the government. If that program, which was introduced in 1969, is so terrific, why was it brought back into the House of Commons in 1973 to be re-endorsed? And hon. members are still talking about it. That program is an absolute, complete and total failure, and 20 years from now we will still be talking about it and there will still be dissension.
The government does not know what it is doing. A Progressive Conservative government would not use bilingualism as an

emotional political issue, because we want to make Canada a better place. When the former minister of national defence had to resign over the government's language policy you can be sure the Liberal government is not acting in the best interests of Canada.
