speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very concerned about certain themes which were brought up during the debate by a good majority of members as well as by certain ministers. The first assertion that worried me is that which some members used to try to give a restrictive interpretation of the Official Languages Act. A great number of members- especially those who are English-speaking-and certain ministers said that the sole objective of this act was to allow citizens of this country, and particularly the francophones, to communicate in French with the federal government.

October 21, 1976
The Address-Mr. De Bane
If this is my reason for being here, I can assure you that this type of fight does not interest me in the least. Indeed, we must consider the fact that a mostly bilingual minority, especially the French-speaking group outside Quebec, will always have a tendency to use the language of the strongest group, particularly when this language corresponds to the real dynamics of the community, and it is not the offer of linguistic services which can go against what we can still call the basic law of economic means. There are those who want to weaken this law to the point of a caricature so as to allow us to communicate in French with the government and to receive a reply in French. It is certainly not worth it to fight for objectives so subtle and insignificant.
The second theme which has often been brought up concerns the inhuman implementation of the Official Languages Act. On this subject, I would like to recall that the implementation of the Official Languages Act was negotiated with the Public Service Alliance, the union which represents civil servants, and unless I am mistaken, I have not often heard the union complain about the implementation of the act, since it was done with its full agreement. On the other hand the commissioner of Official Languages himself has concluded after many investigations that if there are in fact some terrible examples of implementation, the percentage of such occurrences under this policy is really insignificant.
The other theme which was often touched upon concerns the fact that the implementation of this act has been much too rapid. I would like to quote a few figures to show that, since the statement made by the Right Hon. L. B. Pearson about 15 years ago, far from being rapid, advances concerning linguistic equality have been extremely slow. It is therefore useless to put on safety belts since everything is happening at a very slow pace.
In 1976 a mere 12 per cent of federal civil servants are working in their mother tongue which is French. If you look at French-speaking Canadians, there are six times as many- almost 75 per cent-who can work in their mother tongue. If we look at the National Capital area only 7 per cent of the positions require French proficiency while in this city which is supposed to reflect the language duality of our country, more than 66 per cent of the positions require English proficiency only.
In fact, according to a study made by the Treasury Board in 1975, the majority of French-speaking Canadians working in the National Capital area must do so in English. In the province of Quebec, more than 40 per cent of the positions require English proficiency. I am not even talking about French-speaking persons who must work exclusively in English in the province of Quebec, which is true for 12 per cent of those in the so-called technical category. Of course there is even worse: like the Air Canada repair workshop where the use of French has always been completely forbidden.

I wish to quote a few figures about the development of the situation in 1974 and two years later, that is today. At the Agriculture Department, in 1974 only 5.6 per cent of the management was French-speaking and today, in 1976, it is 5.3 per cent. At the Canadian Livestock Feed Board, the Francophones were 3.4 per cent in 1974 against 3.5 per cent today. In the Customs and Excise Division of National Revenue we held 26 per cent of management positions two years ago and today 20 per cent. In the Taxation Division 9.5 per cent of the management were French-speaking three years ago and, today, 6 per cent. In the Consumer and Corporate Affairs Department, 14.8 per cent of the management was Frenchspeaking in 1974 and today this figure has dropped to a mere 9 per cent. Two years ago the Communications Department included 10.9 per cent of French-speaking scientists and today they are even less than that. The Canadian Transportation Commission had 16 per cent of Francophones two years ago and today they have 14 per cent. At National Defence, the percentage of French-speaking employed in a managerial capacity was 4.3, now it is 4.2; to put it another way, out of 24 members of management there was only one French-speaking Canadian. In the Environment Department with 53 management positions two years ago, ten were held by French-speaking persons. Today there is one more Francophone and 11 Anglophones, so this obviously reduces substantially the percentage of French-speaking employees. At Energy, Mines and Resources, quite an important department, two years ago we had 24 English-speaking and two French-speaking members of management. Today the management of that department boasts 31 English-speaking and still only two French-speaking members. At the Department of External Affairs, there were eleven positions two years ago, one French-speaking employee; today, the situation is the same. At the Department of Finance, only two out of 27 management positions were held by French-speaking persons. Today the situation is exactly the same. At the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, French-speaking employees represent 13 per cent of the personnel. At the Department of Urban Affairs, they represented 18 per cent of management two years ago and they have now shrunk to 6 per cent.
The B and B Commission pointed out the limited involvement of French-speaking employees at the intermediate and higher levels of the public service, the almost exclusive use of English as a working language and the gradual acculturation of the French-speaking civil servants. And some dare say today, notwithstanding these public figures, that we are going too fast. So much for that when it comes to language equalit-yin Ottawa; I am just as concerned about the situation in the province of Quebec where, according to some members, French unilingualism is the order of the day.
A French-speaking person wishing to take up a career in major industry in Quebec faces a dilemma. He feels he will often have to choose between his own promotion and the gradual loss of his linguistic and cultural identity. Even more, this person deeply feels he is alienated.
October 21, 1976

More than half the managerial staff of large firms think that a French Canadian who succeeds in a big company should be more English than French. And the firms which are prepared to appoint French-speaking Canadians to key positions always require at least three conditions: the candidates must be perfectly fluent in English, they must accept to be transferred outside Quebec and they must carry out their activity exactly like their English-speaking fellow employees, that is they must think and act in English.
If we look at the average income derived from work by salaried people in Quebec according to the ethnic origin, we notice that French Canadians rank just above the natives. Even more, with equal instruction, French Canadians earn less than other groups. It is to French Canadians that education benefits the least and the gains they have when going from the elementary to the secondary and the university level are even less than those of other groups.
Inside large Canadian manufacturing industries, we see fewer and fewer French Canadians as we go up the hierarchy. In Montreal, French Canadians make up 60 per cent of the staff but only 17 per cent of the executive, which is of 83 per cent English speaking. Ninety per cent of Canadian immigrants in the Montreal region adopt English as their new Canadian language and send their children to English schools even though they live in a province and a city where French is the language of the majority.
When the French-speaking population will have dropped to the rank of a minority in what is the only French-speaking metropolis in North America, something which may happen at the turn of the century at the rate we are going, future prospects will be irreversibly jeopardized for the French-speaking community of North America. We cannot therefore think of French Canada's future without first solving this problem. The present solution is untenable in the long run because it entails the genocide of the French speaking people.
In Quebec, blue collar workers come from the local labour force but three quarters of the positions with an annual salary of over $25,000 are taken up by administrators with Englishspeaking background. In Quebec, with the exception of Montreal, 30 per cent of the executives are English and they hold 80 per cent of the higher ranking positions even though they represent only about 7 per cent of the labour force. More than 96 per cent of French-speaking executives are bound by contract to be bilingual, whereas half of the English-speaking employees are not compelled to know French.
The case is even worse in Montreal, where 86 per cent of the English-speaking persons earning more than $25,000 a year are unilingual. The B and B Commission has reported that the English-speaking minority in Quebec earned the highest wages in all of Canada. Nowhere else do English-speaking workers earn as much as in Quebec. As noted in the report of the commission on the status of the French language and linguistic rights in Quebec, a royal commission set up by the Quebec government under the chairmanship of Mr. Jean-Denis Gen-dron, and I quote:

Even though they are relatively few in number, the English-speaking residents of Quebec succeed in giving their mother tongue a usage status equal in importance to that of French. It is obvious then that francophones bear the cost of their language when the moment comes to set up the necessary contacts between both communities, particularly in labour relations.
Mr. Speaker, individually, within each generation since 1760, thousands of French Canadians join or try to join the English population of North America. In other Canadian provinces and in the United States, over two million are now totally integrated into the Anglo-American mass. Within the very borders of the province of Quebec, that individual assimilation process has been going on for two centuries, but with a great deal of difficulty, because French Canadians always made up and still make up the majority of the Quebec population. They always kept sight of the fact that they represent a community, a society, nay, a separate nation.
Now, the latter, as such, has been living a self-contained existence for three and a half centuries in the St. Lawrence Valley. We are beginning to realize both in French and English Canada that we must immediately give up our illusions of yester years. Canada will not be populated by a French-speaking majority as Quebec had long hoped for. On the other hand, the survival of French Canadians as a distinct community in Quebec is an accomplished fact. Any realistic policy must rest on the realization that two major groups or two nations now co-exist in Canada. Such is the wish of history.
The political philosophy of French-speaking people in Quebec is no longer that of a group who, having survived linguistically, would be contented with a minority status. Therefore two conclusions must be drawn: first, the need to put an end to the misconception on which the association of French- and English-speaking Canadians within confederation has been resting up to the present day and, second, the need to grant official recognition to the national rights of French Canadians.
Yielding to the will of the nation which had conquered the St. Lawrence Valley, the descendants of the vanquished in 1760 had to accept their fate as a minority group. The few concessions which their leaders gained concerning the use of French, the preservation of civil rights in Quebec and the protection of Catholic schools made this acceptance easier. It remains nevertheless that French Canadians were permanently reduced as a community to a subordinate position in the country built by the conquerors of 1760 and their heirs.

To the worries and distress of most of the peoples of the earth in this era of violence, both physical and symbolical, we must add those of a people which strives for its survivance and its development. One day, the crisis bursts out, the blow is hard. The next day, you wake up all alone, disarmed, reduced to nothing, contemplating a national catastrophy in which all our hopes for unity and fraternity were destroyed. The national unity of Canada is now greatly threatened. It hurts, it really hurts when you see yourself a prisoner, unable to guide your own destiny, the prisoner of a play written in advance.
I realize more and more that our behaviour shows a false confidence, it contributes to create a situation which is in fact artificial because we try with all possible means to evade a sometimes unduly disturbing reality. Mr. De Bank Quebecers make up a community whose majority is composed of francophone Canadians. This Community has its own history, its own institutions, its own culture, its own way of life, its own values and its members are linked by unbreakable ties. We can therefore talk about a Quebec society or a Quebec nation. Each Canadian province has indeed its own people which differ from those of the next, but it is only in Quebec that it is possible to find a nation, in the sociological sense of the word. Whether we like it or not, Quebecers see themselves as Quebecers first, Canadians second. There are of course other nations in Canada, the Eskimos, the Indians. It is not the existence of a Quebec nation which is questioned here, but the principle whether every nation has the right to be necessarily independent, without consideration for any other nation.
The people from Quebec have always been nationalists. Before the sixties, Quebec nationalism was rather conservative, arising largely from a defence reflex and from an insecurity feeling which we must not be ashamed of. Any people in the world in the same situation as Quebecers would have behaved in a similar way. As for the new nationalism, its history is still too recent to enable us to place a final label on it. However, it seems much more dynamic than before, more open, in a word, more positive. One thing is certain, it is here to stay. All those who think that the mixing of ideas and initiatives which has taken and is still taking place in Quebec is a temporary phenomenon are making a big mistake.
We do not argue that each Quebecer as an individual is clearly aware of all those differences we are trying to emphasize. We do not contend either that all Quebecers unanimously agree on political measures to take. On the contrary, there are

considerable differences of opinion. This is quite normal. However, the fact is that the Quebec society represents a separate entity and gradually, it understands that its full development requires a certain freedom and the presence of psychological conditions which are not present now.
One can always argue, through ignorance or to alleviate one's conscience, that within the present constitutional framework Quebec can act almost as it wants in areas under its jurisdiction and that it rests with it to assume all its responsibilities. This line of thinking, which reassures those who are concerned about possible changes, is deceitful. It is only true for legislative matters which undoubtedly are and have always been recognized by everybody as being under the exclusive jurisdiction of the province.
We are confronted by the following situation. On one hand, the Quebec society wants to assert its authority, find its identity, do what it wants within the Canadian framework. This movement is not only powerful but it is here for good. For some years it has been the position of my party that not only should there be two separate ministers fulfilling these responsibilities, but that there should be two departments, distinct and separate, one for fisheries, and one for the environment. We repeat that position. We see no reason at all to change our position in this regard. We made our views known some years ago and events since then have only reinforced our belief, namely, that this is a proper and justifiable position.
It is apparent to us that the government is either unaware of the basic difference of these two departments or, in the alternative, is so completely indifferent to their individual importance that it chooses to reject the national and international implications connected with the operations of these two units of the government.
Surely one need not be an expert to appreciate that the nature of Fisheries is economic, social, and even cultural. On the other hand, one does not need great perceptual insight to appreciate that with respect to the environment we are dealing basically with scientific research. By their very nature, activities concerning Fisheries and the environment should be distinct and separate from each other. In ignoring this fact the government has undoubtedly weakened both sectors, at a time, unhappily, when both should have been strengthened.
One might say that combining these two activities under one minister is justiFied in terms of restraint. If the government had so ordered its economic priorities as to indicate some justiFication for this uniFication of function that would have been fine. But those priorities have not been made known; they have not been forthcoming. It seems to me that, in the absence of such justification, and having regard to the size of the present cabinet, such alleged restriction in government spending can only be an excuse for this combination, not a reason. Only the government's unwillingness to embark on progressive action and to undertake its responsibilities in the Fields of fisheries and the environment has led it along this course.
If I have time I shall return to this topic and deal with the very structure of the department. At the moment I want to deal with what the Speech from the Throne had to say about the environment. I suppose hon. members opposite would be only too happy if I said absolutely nothing about the topic, because that is exactly what the Speech from the Throne said-nothing. It said absolutely nothing about the environment. We heard of the necessity to place further emphasis on research and development of renewable energy resources, but nothing about measures to regulate exploration and development on federal lands. Again, no mention whatsoever was made of environmental concerns. Yes, we did hear about native peoples' land claims in the James Bay region, but nothing about environmental concerns in that important region. We even heard about our international responsibilities in terms of environmental protection, but nothing about our national responsibilities-and all this from a government which has professed over the years to be concerned about our environment.
In the throne speech of September, 1968, the government talked about the broad importance of the problem of pollution. In October, 1969, in his speech following the throne speech of that year, the Prime Minister spoke about the increasing concern with regard to the environment, about the ruthless destruction of a landscape and the useless pollution of air and water. He spoke of determination to overcome noise, noxious fumes, and the pollution from industrial waste, and said:
First of all, we will never sacrifice, in the name of progress, a clean and healthy environment to industrial or commercial development.
The year 1970 was a vintage year for the environment. The Speech from the Throne had this to say:
Pollution is a many-headed hydra and requires action in many forms. You will be asked to consider bills intended to deal with pollution in two of its aspects: in the ocean and in the atmosphere. More pressing than any single step or steps, however, is the need to co-ordinate and consolidate our efforts in an effective fashion. There will be proposed the establishment of a department to be concerned with the environment and the husbanding of those renewable resources that are a part of and dependent upon it.
This was welcome news for the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) who then was leader of the opposition.
The then minister of fisheries was absolutely glowing on October 15, 1970, when he said:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words this afternoon about the establishment of a new Department of Environmental Affairs, and I should like to say at the outset that shaping our Canadian environment is the biggest challenge we face in the 1970's. It is a bigger challenge than unemployment. It is a bigger challenge than inflation. It is a bigger issue than pensions or skyjacking or the FLQ. To many Canadians it is a bigger challenge than all of our financial and social problems put together.
It was the first minister of the environment who said that exactly six years ago last week. Since then it has been all downhill. In 1972 there was just passing reference made. In
1973	there was one brief reference in the throne speech. In
1974	the only reference was a wish to enhance the environment of cities and towns. In September, 1974, there was an almost seeming obsession with the environment. We had an overwhelming two sentences in the throne speech devoted to this subject.
If we need to look for any further evidence of the government's disinterest in the Department of the Environment we have only to realize that there have been four ministers in 24 months. Nothing in this government changes more than ministers of the environment, except economic policy. Therefore one can hardly be surprised at the lack of policy direction which results from this constant changing at the ministerial level.
This is all the more tragic when one appreciates that the Department of the Environment appeared to have been created in 1970 in an air of responsibility, concern, and even optimism. For the first time we recognized the inter-relationships among water, air and soil pollution. For the first time we acknowledged the importance of environmental considerations in planning government programs.
The Prime Minister on October 9, 1970, said that the new department was intended, and I quote:

October 21, 1976

-to bring under the direction of a single minister the principal government activities relating to environmental quality in general, and pollution in particular.
Six years ago Canadians believed we were on the right track and the government was indeed concerned about this problem. I take no satisfaction in saying that perhaps the creation of the Department of the Environment was really little more than another of the Prime Minister's intellectual daydreams or, perhaps more accurately, his reaction to the situation in the 1960's when environmental concerns were the fashion of the day, a fad, an emotional reaction, and sometimes even overreaction in the sixties, mainly by young people and community activists who found a convenient and sometimes temporary cause, who found activities that were attractive to the media and politicians alike. I do not say this unkindly because it was their idealism and enthusiasm and vigor that gave birth to the environmental movement of today. However, a decade later the same situation does not exist and the government, with a great sigh of relief, says to itself well, thank heavens, we need not worry about environment any more.
What the government has failed to realize is that environmental concerns have not gone away. They have, in a short ten years, matured remarkably. Community groups, instead of fishing rubber boots out of rivers, are working with research scientists in our universities. Whole new faculties of environmental sciences have sprung up. Protest marchers of the sixties now prepare educational video tapes, and work quietly but effectively with our school children, service clubs, and so on.
Pollution protest rallies have been replaced by national and international environment seminars. Pollution protesters have become planners, and I commend them for it. May I give two examples.
In my riding of Perth-Wilmot an environmental group formed by students at Northwestern Secondary School is involved in the concerns resulting from the planning of new hydro lines and highways.
On a national scale I point out the Canadian Wildlife Federation which, ten years ago, with a two-man staff, preoccupied itself with writing protest letters and briefs to elected representatives. Today that federation, at the national level in research staff alone has a staff of eight, including a biologist, an environmental scientist, and an economist, all with high academic credentials. In addition they have an impressive inventory of research people and are now preoccupied with the environmental planning process. They are able to challenge professional scientific reports on such difficult subjects as the MacKenzie Valley pipeline and the Garrison dam.
It is tragic that the government has not matured along with those it purports to represent.
I might mention that this department must preoccupy itself with environmental concerns. A few of these, in no particular order of priority, are coastal ocean petroleum drilling, shipping and the handling of hazardous cargo, environmental protection of the north, protection of the ozone layer and other atmospheric concerns, water quality and quantity problems, and nuclear waste disposal. Other challenges are found in the
Adjournment Debate
department's relationship to other governmental bodies, such as other departments and other governments.
In offshore drilling, for example, we find Energy, Mines and Resources responsible in areas south of the sixtieth parallel; Indian and Northern Affairs responsible north of sixty; provincial governments likely responsible within three or 12 miles off our coasts, and federal responsibility beyond these limits.
In terms of its responsibility with regard to relationships with provincial governments, the conflicts and the problems are limitless. At the federal level maybe we have assumed too much responsibility, for historic reasons which now have disappeared. Now certainly should be the occasion for this department to have the time and resources to examine whether other governments, particularly provincial governments, should become more active, or may indeed wish a more vital role in environmental matters.
There is one other matter. No department could welcome more the freedom of information policy than the Department of the Environment. I commend them in terms of the Beaufort report which they released to concerned municipalities. It would bring great credit to this department if they would pursue such a policy without the compulsion of the proposed legislation.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, there is a challenge to be faced in terms of the difficulties of melding what have been essentially individual approaches to particular resource issues into major environmental objectives and then fitting these objectives into national priorities.
I suggest to the new minister that this department need not of necessity be a homogeneous totally inter-related department. Some of the structural changes that I see in the department, in my judgment are not healthy and are not functioning well. subtopic: BANK ACT-POSSIBILITY OF AMENDMENT FACILITATING APPOINTMENT OF WOMEN AS DIRECTORS

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: BANK ACT-POSSIBILITY OF AMENDMENT FACILITATING APPOINTMENT OF WOMEN AS DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the brief time I have at my disposal I want to demonstrate for the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) that I

October 21, 1976
Adjournment Debate
am about to speak extemporaneously without the aid of mirrors or eyeglasses. I will try to make a point in which she will be very interested, that is, the question which I raised on October 15 with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in regard to faciliting the appointment of women as directors of chartered banks in Canada. I see my friend has stayed and will give me moral and actual support in the particular representation which I made to the Minister of Finance at that time.
The minister indicated in his response, in a positive but rather general way, that he would be giving some consideration to an amendment to the Bank Act which would allow women to be elected more easily as directors of our chartered banks. He also referred to the fact the amendments might also make it easier for other people in our country to become bank directors.
I see the parliamentary secretary is here representing the minister. I want to bring to his attention some information which he may in fact be possessed of already, but which I alluded to in my question.
A study was sponsored by the Advisory Council on the Status of Women and the Canadian Bankers' Association, and prepared by Marianne Bossen, entitled "Employment in Chartered Banks: 1969-1975." In 1975, 122,572 men and women were employed by all branches of the chartered banks in Canada. At least 72 per cent of these employees were women. Marianne Bossen reports that the position of women in the banking industry has improved both quantitatively and qualitatively since 1969. This is principally because of the rapid expansion of the banking industry in those years.
According to this study, some banks have introduced more enlightened policies and the measure of responsibility given to women at every level has increased. Be that as it may, the study notes that in 1975 no women earned more than $30,000 a year, whereas 442 men did; only three women earned more than $20,000, while 1,279 men did; 32 per cent of the women employed earned between $6,000 and $6,900, while 73 per cent of them earned less than $8,000.
The other statistic 1 should bring to the attention of the House is this: as of October, 1976, six women hold corporate directorships in chartered banks compared with a total of 220 men who are directors of Canada's five big chartered banks.
My colleague, the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather), who is the spokesman for our party on the status of women, has this session brought forward a private member's bill which would have the effect of repealing subsection (2) of section 18 of the Bank Act thereby removing the necessity for a bank director to hold a prohibitively costly amount of stock in order to qualify. This is really the nub of the problem. The removal of that subsection would democratize directorships of the chartered banks, and I believe it is not asking too much to urge the government to consider bringing in the necessary amendment. The government would find all the opposition parties agreeable to making a quick disposition of the legislation.
I hope the minister and the government will not wait until the white paper on banking has been considered and we go through the whole rather tedious and lengthy process of considering revisions to the Bank Act now that the ten-year period has expired. I see the parliamentary secretary is ready to stand up and say that this amendment will be brought in during the present session. At least I hope that this will be the case.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BANK ACT-POSSIBILITY OF AMENDMENT FACILITATING APPOINTMENT OF WOMEN AS DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, representations in favour of the bill to which the hon. member referred have not come only from the other side of the House. I am glad to tell the hon. member that similar representations have come from this side of the House, as well as from officials responsible for advising on the status of women.
The advancement of the status of women is a major goal of the government, as has already been shown in many ways. Laws which discriminated against women have been changed. A human rights code has been proposed to afford recourse to women when they are the victims of discrimination in areas where the federal authority can reach. As to the deplorable statistics about banks which the hon. member put on record, I am glad to remind him that banks are under federal jurisdiction and that this human rights code will cover banks. I hope the code will receive rapid passage.
I am not proud to remind the House that in 1970, when the Royal Commission on the Status of Women made its recommendations, there was only one woman in the SX category of the Canadian public service. But today there are 30. This has been the result of positive action to give women a fair chance. In order in Council appointments, women have also begun to get the recognition that simple justice requires.
The government has also campaigned actively to change public attitudes which have been a large factor in holding women back. How far the public attitude has progressed was shown by the genuine and healthy outrage felt toward the dinosaur attitudes of some conservative bankers. To their credit the bankers have quickly learned something of the consequences of writing off half of our population as possible directors of banks. The Canadian people simply will not accept rationalizations for the absence of women from bank boards.
The white paper on banking legislation proposes specific qualifications for directors in line with the general corporate law, and this may obviate the need for substantial, direct financial interest in a bank by its directors. This will help to open the door to many capable women who cannot now qualify. As the minister said in the House, we are ready to look at the question as the new legislation proceeds.

SOCIAL SECURITY-RECIPROCITY OF PENSIONS BETWEEN CANADA AND CERTAIN COUNTRIES-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight because of an unsatisfactory answer that I received to a question that I asked today about amendments in the proposed old age security bill.
[Mr. Hnatyshyn.)
October 21, 1976

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-RECIPROCITY OF PENSIONS BETWEEN CANADA AND CERTAIN COUNTRIES-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: You mean yesterday.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-RECIPROCITY OF PENSIONS BETWEEN CANADA AND CERTAIN COUNTRIES-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Yesterday. I should like to put on the record a bit of the history of this bill. On April 14 the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) announced that he was going to bring in legislation that would enable us to have reciprocity of pensions between Canada and some western European countries, including the United Kingdom. On October 13, as soon as parliament resumed, my hon. friend from Hamilton West asked the minister when he was going to bring in the bill affecting, among other things, residency and reciprocal agreements affecting persons who have earned pensions overseas. The answer then, believe it or not, was as follows, as reported at page 19 of Hansard:
The bill is being drafted and I hope I will be able to table it in the House for first reading in the next few months.
Those are the words of the Minister of National Health and Welfare on October 13, almost exactly the same words as he used when on April 14 he was boasting that he was going to bring in this bill in the next few months.
This caused me to ask my later question about the bill, and it also caused me to include this subject in my speech on October 15 when I pointed out that, according to the minister, he said that the project had been discussed with his colleagues, if he remembered well, at the last federal-provincial conference held in June and no objection was made to the project either at the June conference or afterwards. He went on to say that consequently he thought we could undertake with confidence a study of this project.
As the days go by and the situation gets worse, not only does he not have the bill ready but the minister is talking about having a study of the project made. This is a very serious situation, Mr. Speaker. If one considers the twin devils of inflation and devaluation, particularly so far as people who came here from Britain a few years ago are concerned, one can realize the desperate circumstances in which they find themselves today.
I had some research on this subject done today and I should like to point out the following. A couple who came to Canada in 1965 on a pension of 100 pounds sterling a month would have drawn a cheque worth $301. The cost of living then stood at 80 in the consumer price index. Today that same pension cheque would be worth $161, barely half what it was worth in 1965, and cost of living on the same scale has gone from 80 to 150. This means that this couple would be able to buy only one third of the items they were able to buy 11 years ago.
What have these people done to deserve a fate like that? These are the very people that we maintain are the rockbed of our society, people who saved to pay into a pension plan so they could comfortably survive in their old age. What have we done to them? We have taken away two-thirds of the value of their pension.
Adjournment Debate
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) and I have been writing letters to the Minister of National Health and Welfare about this subject since the first day we came to the House. We have received nothing but procrastination and put-offs from him. First he blamed the British for not making their pensions convertible. Both the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and myself wrote and asked the British government what was the holdup. The reply we received indicated that the holdup had resulted because the Canadian government was dragging its feet on this matter.
Let me go back to this set of tables to point out what has happened in the last four years since we came to parliament. Some four years ago this mythical couple had an income of $263 a month when the cost of groceries was $106. In only four years their cheques have decreased from $263 to $161, while the cost of their groceries has increased from $106 to $150. The cost of groceries has gone up about 50 per cent while the pension has gone down something like one third. It is absolutely impossible for these people to go on this way.
I was taken in on April 14 by the minister. I believed he was going to bring this legislation in, as he said, in a few months. We had a summer recess of a few months and it should have been the most simple thing in the world to get the bill ready. Now the minister says the bill is being drafted. I thought it was being drafted on April 14. When I was questioned by my constituents I said I trusted and believed the minister and thought the bill would be in probably the day we got back to parliament. Instead the government has spent the summer drafting a bill to amend the Historic Sites and Monuments Act. That is apparently the priority of the government, not the senior citizens, Or the people trying to exist on pensions that have been cut in half at a time when food costs have increased 50 per cent.
The government is apparently very much concerned about spending its time contemplating the bill on historic sites and monuments, which was given first reading today, whereas the bill in respect of pensions, according to the minister, is being drafted, had he hopes to be able to introduce it in the House for first reading in the next few months.
Can the parliamentary secretary give any hope to these people that this year, perhaps before Christmas, they will be able to get a pension equivalent to the one they were getting when they came to this country ten years ago?

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. McRae (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-RECIPROCITY OF PENSIONS BETWEEN CANADA AND CERTAIN COUNTRIES-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) for this question. I think we all share the desire to get this thing out of the way. I do not think I can give him the assurance that it will be out of the way by Christmas, but I can certainly assure him that it will be within a few months, perhaps shortly after Christmas.
In announcing on April 14 the government's intention to amend the Old Age Security Act the minister indicated that one of its effects would be to enhance Canada's ability to enter into international social security agreements. As the act now
358

October 21, 1976
Adjournment Debate
stands it does not provide for international agreements, yet the several countries which have expressed an interest in having reciprocal social agreements with Canada have all insisted that the OAS program be included in such agreements alongside the Canada Pension Plan. This has complicated the whole issue.
It follows, therefore, that the negotiation of such agreements cannot be undertaken until the proposed legislation amending the Old Age Security Act has been enacted by parliament. I would add that, taken as a whole, the proposals formulated by other countries to date cover the whole field of social security as understood in Europe. In the Canadian context, international agreements could, therefore, involve programs which come under provincial jurisdiction, such as workmen's compensation and hospital and medical care insurance. Hon. members will be happy, therefore, to know that considerable progress has been made both in the drafting of the amendments to the OAS Act and in the necessary interdepartmental and federal-provincial consultations.
Several hon. members, both orally and in writing, have requested an indication of those countries likely to be involved in such negotiations. Our tendency would be to negotiate first with those countries which have been pressing Canada for agreements-the United Kingdom, Italy and the United States-since the highest number of potential beneficiaries residing in Canada would be covered by agreements with those countries.
France also might be included in this list, having shown some interest. I wish to emphasize, however, as the minister did in the House on April 14, that Canada is prepared, in due course, to enter into agreements with all interested countries whenever this is in the interests of Canada and of residents of Canada. In conclusion, I hope that within the next few months this bill will be proposed and will be put through the House.

SEARCH AND RESCUE-DATE OF TABLING REPORT OF TASK FORCE-REQUEST FOR IMPROVEMENT IN OPERATION OF SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is nice to note that there are two members on the government side here tonight. My topic concerns the unfortunate and tragic loss of 13 seamen some 60 miles off the southeast coast of Newfoundland and the slow reaction in response to the distress call of the motor vessel Gabriella, which prompted my question yesterday, along with that of my colleague from St. John's East. We request again, in addition to the many representations we made during the last session, that our air search and rescue capability be expanded and, more specifically, that elements of the force be deployed to the province of Newfoundland.
For too many months now we have been hearing the same answers from the minister. On December 5, 1975,4he minister related to me in a letter that the review of the national search

and rescue policy had been completed and that the necessary implementation documents were being prepared in consultation with the Department of National Defence, and that he expected that the revised policy would be ready for submission to Cabinet in April of 1976 following approval by himself and his colleague, the Minister of National Defence.
Then in April of this year it was noted in the minister's release that a Canadian coastguard task force had reviewed the national search and rescue policy and that the revised policy was expected to be ready for submission to cabinet by mid-1976. But here we are in late October, with winter upon us, and no progress, while we are concerned that a repeat of last year's incidents are imminent.
I realize that the implementation of a co-ordinated operation order must be thought out carefully. I realize also that the funding required for the expanded responsibility both in hardware and manpower will be immense. But I say as strongly as I can that there is no reason why part of the force capability cannot be deployed closer to the action. Notwithstanding the minister's reply that the coastguard facilities could not be everywhere awaiting an accident, which would be impossible, surely the almost five-hour period of reaction time from the mainland in the lastest incident, and similar experiences last year, would suggest that attention should be given to the stationing of helicopters in the province of Newfoundland.
Certainly when we consider that we are talking about lives, even with the argument that it would not be of any advantage to have an air search and rescue presence in Newfoundland, it is worth a try for at least a year to see what the result would be. Certainly the stationing of a crew in western central and eastern Newfoundland is worth while if it could prevent the loss of lives. I note the following statement in the minister's release:
It has become evident that, in spite of the provision of additional resources, facilities and co-ordination capabilities over the years, the marine search and rescue organization is no longer adequate.
I hope the minister will discuss this with his colleague responsible for the Department of National Defence.
Time does not permit me to go into detail about the coastguard sea rescue capability but I am interested in an item in the release which states that one of the areas which will receive immediate attention is that dealing with a proposed voluntary coast guard auxiliary and that implementation guidelines would be available this summer. Here we are in October and there are no implementation guidelines.
I should like to make a suggestion to the parliamentary secretary to give to his minister. I think it is worthy of consideration and will have some merit in the planning.
The nature of Newfoundland lends itself to sea orientation, and I suggest that the minister should consider the establishment of an adjunct to the coast guard college to train our youth for careers in the coast guard to supplement the permanent establishment which will be created and, what is more important, to provide employment in line with the job creation

thrust that is due to be announced. More than adequate accommodation is available-it was left to the province by the United States air force-as well as more than adequate classroom space, and all the other infrastructure support that is required. I understand, after checking with the staffing officer at the coast guard college, that they received far more applications than they have vacancies.
I hope the minister will consider this suggestion in line with the expansion of the coast guard, and I hope I will receive a positive response to my proposal for the immediate tabling of the task force report by the Canadian coast guard, and immediate consideration to deploy elements of air search and rescue in Newfoundland so as to ensure that the proper precautions will be taken to alleviate the situation, and proper action will be taken to prevent accidents from occurring in the future.
